An agent is a user account that talks to a language-model server. It is an
ordinary :agent 

account, created by an
administrator as a constituent of that administrator (:game:bot for
:game’s agent :bot), and everything it can do it does with the authority of
that account. A session is a durable conversation with one agent: a small
database value holding the transcript, the usage counters, and a channel —
a pair of streams through which the administrator sends messages and receives
replies.

The layer is deliberately narrow. It connects air to a provider, manages the
context window, and turns text into a reply; the agent does not evaluate air
code, call tools, or stream tokens (see 

Limits).

(as-user :game
  (create-agent :bot provider=:fireworks model="accounts/fireworks/models/llama-v3p3-70b-instruct"
                        api-key="fw_…" system="You are a careful assistant."))
;; => (agent base-url="https://api.fireworks.ai/inference/v1" dialect=:openai
;;           id=:game:bot model="…" provider=:fireworks)

Only an administrator (or air) may create an agent, and only a core user
may; a constituent cannot. The name is one segment and the account is always
:agent’s own id, :<admin>:<name>. (user-kind :game:bot) is :agent,
(agent? :game:bot) is true, and (agents) lists the agent accounts the
caller can see (air sees every agent).

:compatible is the escape hatch for any server that speaks the OpenAI
chat-completions API — a vLLM or Ollama instance, a gateway, a proxy — so
provider=:compatible base-url="http://localhost:8000/v1" reaches a local
model. params= carries anything the dialect does not build itself (a
reserved key such as model or messages raises).

agent-config redacts api-key unless secrets=true.

Warning

The API key is stored verbatim in the agent’s $.config.agent. It is an
ordinary namespace entry, so the ordinary ownership rules protect it: the
agent, its administrator, and air can read it, and a stranger is denied with
(error :permission-denied …). It is nonetheless in the database, so a dump or
backup contains it.

The key is read live from $.config.agent on every call, so
agent-config! rotating it takes effect in sessions that are already open. The
rest of the configuration is snapshotted when a session opens (below).

(val s (open-session :bot))                       ; a new session
(val s (open-session :bot id="s-3f9a1c2d"))       ; reopen an existing one
(val s (open-session :bot model="…" context=200000))  ; new, with overrides

open-session returns a handle:(session id="s-3f9a1c2d" agent=:game:bot owner=:game state=<mut>
         channel=(channel id="c-3f9a1c2d" agent=:game:bot owner=:game
                          state=<mut> in=<stream> out=<stream> in-notify=<stream>))

The handle is a convenience value. The state mutable is the durable root:
it holds the status, the configuration snapshot, the transcript, the usage
counters, the last error, and the three streams. A session is stored behind the
named form agent/<agent>/sessions/<sid> in the agent’s home database, so a
session survives a process restart and can be reopened in a fresh environment
over the same database. The session belongs to the agent, so its administrator
reaches it through the ordinary administrator rules, and air bypasses every
check.

Opening a session validates the configuration: a missing model or API key
raises (error :agent-misconfigured…) at open-session, not at creation. The
snapshot options — provider, dialect, base-url, model, system,
max-tokens, params, context, compact-at, compact-keep, timeout,
retries — become that session’s settings and can differ from the agent’s
record. api-key is not one of them; it is read live.

Sessions are listed for the agent’s administrator; another user is denied by
the access check. A closed session stays readable — its state, its transcript,
and its streams — but a post to it raises (error :stream-closed).

A message posted to a session is either text for the model or a
command:

a string, or any form whose head is not a keyword, is a turn. A string
contributes its contents; anything else is rendered with the ordinary
printer, so (session-post s (list 1 2 3)) sends (1 2 3).

a form whose head is a keyword is a command, handled below.

A turn appends (role=:user text="…") to the transcript, calls the provider,
and appends (role=:assistant text="…"). The reply arrives on the inbox:(session-post s "Summarize the plan.")
(session-fetch s)     ; => (reply text="…" model="…" stop="end_turn"
                      ;           usage=(input=12 output=8 total=20)
                      ;           time=(time "2026-10-30T…"))

session-fetch supports the stream options: timeout=n returns naught when
nothing arrives, and meta=true returns the envelope — the reply with
sender= and time= — instead of the object. channel-ready? and
channel-count poll without blocking. Writes never block unless a bounded
stream is full, and the session’s streams are unbounded.

A failed call posts an error object instead of a reply and leaves the session
usable:

:agent-session

a session value is malformed or lacks its streams

:agent-command

an unknown command

A 429 or a 5xx is retried retries times with exponential backoff before it is
reported; another 4xx is immediate. The key is never included in an error or a
message.

A keyword-headed message is a command; it never enters the transcript.

(:stop) sets the session to :paused: later posts queue up and no worker
reads them until (session-resume s), which reopens the session and drains the
queue. (:reset), (:system), and (:model) change the session only, never
the agent’s record.

A channel is the pair of streams a session is built on. Directions are from the
owner’s point of view — the administrator who opened the session:

field

direction

out

the owner’s outbox: a message posted here goes to the agent

in

the owner’s inbox: the agent’s replies arrive here

in-notify

the private copy queue for the owner’s hook

form

meaning

(channel? x)

whether x is a channel handle

(channel-post ch msg)

append to out and wake the agent

(channel-fetch ch meta=false timeout=n)

take from in

(channel-ready? ch)

whether a reply is waiting

(channel-count ch)

the queued replies

(channel-hook! ch form)

install the on-receive hook

(channel-unhook! ch)

remove it

(channel-close! ch)

close the session’s streams

The channel handle carries the state mutable, so a hook installed after a
handle was made is seen through it. The streams are created by and owned by the
agent, so they carry its owner-only ACL; the administrator reaches them through
the ordinary administrator rules and air bypasses the checks.

A hook lets the owner react to each reply without polling:(as-user :game
  (def (log-reply ?msg) (post $.replies (get msg :text))))
(as-user :game (session-hook! s 'log-reply))

A hook gets a copy. When the agent delivers a reply, an installed hook
receives a copy while the original stays queued for session-fetch, so the
two never steal from each other.

It runs as the receiving end’s owner, in the registering namespace. The
hook form is evaluated in the namespace where it was installed and with the
owner’s identity, so (current-user) is the owner and a def that exists
only in that namespace resolves.

It is called as a function of the message: (form msg) — a symbol naming
a def, a replacement-rule lambda, or any form.

Its errors are contained. A failing hook is recorded in
(session-info s)'s last-hook-error (as the air error object) and the next
reply still reaches both the hook and the session.

Installing replaces and drains. session-hook! discards stale copies
before it installs, and a copy that was already waiting when the hook was
replaced runs the new hook; channel-unhook! stops delivery. Only the
owner (or air) may install or remove one.

The copy queue is unbounded. A hook slower than the replies lets
in-notify grow.

The agent end has a built-in on-receive — its worker consumes the outbox
directly — so no user-installed hook exists on that side.

The estimate is a characters-over-four heuristic over the system prompt and the
transcript, floored by the last response’s exact input-token count; it is
deliberately approximate, so compaction may trigger a little early or late.

With context= set, the worker compacts before a call when the estimate
crosses compact-at × context. Compaction keeps the system prompt and the last
compact-keep entries verbatim and replaces everything older with a single
(role=:summary text="…") entry, which is sent as part of the system prompt
(Anthropic) or as a leading system message (OpenAI-compatible). The
summarizer’s own usage counts toward the session totals. The request’s
max-tokens is clamped down when the estimate plus the reply cap would exceed
the window; if even compaction leaves no room, the turn fails with
(error :agent-context …). (:compact) compacts on demand, with or without a
configured window; (:context) reports the numbers.

Without context=, nothing compacts automatically and the transcript grows
until the provider refuses it.

Sessions, transcripts, and channels are database values. A restart loses
nothing, but it also leaves no worker running: no process starts a worker
until a message arrives. A session is woken by a post
(session-post/channel-post), by open-session with a queued message, or by
(session-resume s). Messages posted while the process was down are therefore
processed on the next post or the next open-session/session-resume.

One worker runs per session per process; a second process over the same
database is not coordinated with the first, so it is best to treat a session as
belonging to one running process at a time.

No streaming: a reply arrives whole.

No tools or function calling, and the agent does not evaluate air code.

The token estimate is a heuristic, not a tokenizer.

Sessions accumulate; there is no purge or garbage collection yet.

A form is a collection: a sequence of elements and a map of key–value entries.
The same verbs operate on both, and a scalar is treated as its own sole
sequence element, so collection code rarely needs a special case for one value.
This chapter covers access and update, the wildcard key, the whole collection
surface, the higher-order verbs, threading and pipelines, and traversal by
depth. 

The data model describes the form itself;


Tables and 

Tensors add their own path grammars.

count is the number of sequence elements; length is the number of
entries, sequence elements plus map entries. A scalar is a singleton
((count 5) is 1, (count naught) is 0), a table reports its rows, and a
tensor its elements.(count (a=1 b=2))       # => 0
(length (a=1 b=2))      # => 2
(count (1 2 a=3))       # => 2
(in 2 (1 2 3))          # => true       (member? is the same with its arguments in the other order)
(contains? (a=1) :a)    # => true
(haskey (a=1) :a)       # => true
(keys (a=1 b=2))        # => (:a :b)
(vals (a=1 b=2))        # => (1 2)
(empty? ())             # => true

get takes a path of keys. An integer indexes the sequence (1-based); a
negative integer counts from the end; 0 is the whole form; and n + 1 is
the append position in a setter. A keyword names a map entry, and a bare
symbol key is read as a keyword:(get (a b c) 2)          # => b
(get (a b c) -1)         # => c
(get (a=1 b=2) :b)       # => 2
(get (a=1 b=2) b)        # => 2
(get ((a=1) (a=2)) 2 :a) # => 2       (a path walks the form)
(get 5 1)                # => 5       (a scalar is its own sole element)

The . accessor is pure sugar: f.a.b is (get f :a :b), f.:x is
(get f :x), and ... splices ((f a... b)). Its keys are held, so a bare
suffix is the literal keyword and f.a ignores a variable a; ~ evaluates
one key, so f.~k is (get f (preval k)) and f.~a.b is
(get f (preval a) :b). A leading-dot atom such as .util.a is a namespace
path and reads as (get . :util :a) (see 

Namespaces).

hold=true makes a root hold transparent: the path then indexes the content
without reducing intermediate values, and the result is held. This works for
any form that keeps its arguments as data, not only a hold:(get (' f (1 + 2)) 2 hold=true)     # => (' 1 + 2)
(get (part add 10) 2 hold=true)     # => 'add

The hold- family is the same idea as a prefix: hold-get, hold-nth,
hold-with, hold-wout, hold-push, hold-push-in, hold-join,
hold-join-in, hold-update, hold-update-in, and hold-held? operate on a
held form’s content and return the result held, with hold= selecting the
result’s heldness. See 

Holds.

The lone : names every entry of a level: each sequence element in order,
then each map value in canonical key order (the printer’s order; air does not
preserve the order in which keys were written).

In get it selects the whole level and maps the rest of the path over each
entry, so the result is an ordinary sequence and map values lose their keys:
(get ((a=1) (a=2)) : :a) is (1 2), (get (a=1 b=2) :) is (1 2), and
(get (1 2 a=3) :) is (1 2 3).

In with a scalar is broadcast to every entry ((with (a=1 b=2) : 9) is
(a=9 b=9)) and a container supplies one value per entry in that same
canonical order ((with (b=2 a=1) : (7 8)) is (a=7 b=8)), keeping each
sequence position and map key in place.

In wout and drop it removes every entry, and as an intermediate step it
applies the rest of the path to each one
((wout ((a=1 x=0) (a=2 x=0)) : :x) is ((a=1) (a=2))).

Map entries can be unintuitive. Map values are paired in canonical key
order, not source order, so write the values in the order the printer would
show the keys. On a mixed level the sequence elements always come first, so
(with (1 2 a=3) : (7 8 9)) is (7 8 a=9). A scalar sets every entry, but a
one-element form is one value, not a broadcast, so (with (a=1 b=2) : (9))
raises — air never collapses (9) into 9. A table keeps its own meaning for
: (all rows or all columns), and a lone : raises on a table path.

Every update is pure: it returns a new form and leaves its argument unchanged.(with (a=1 b=2) :a 9)              # => (a=9 b=2)
(with ((a=1) (a=2)) 2 :a 9)        # => ((a=1) (a=9))
(wout (a=1 b=2) :a)                # => (b=2)
(drop (a=1 b=2) :a)                # => (b=2)
(update (a=1) :a inc)              # => (a=2)
(update-in (a=(b=1)) :a :b inc)    # => (a=(b=2))
(push (1 2) 3 4)                   # => (1 2 3 4)
(pop (1 2 3))                      # => (1 2)
(push-in (a=(1 2)) :a 3)           # => (a=(1 2 3))
(join (1 2) (3 4))                 # => (1 2 3 4)
(join (a=1) (b=2))                 # => (a=1 b=2)
(merge (a=1) (a=2 b=3))            # => (a=2 b=3)

with takes a path and then one value; wout removes the entry at a path;
update and update-in replace the subform with (f old) (a missing
update-in key is naught to f); push appends; pop removes the last
sequence element; join concatenates sequences and merges maps. An integer key
of n + 1 in a setter appends. insert inserts at an index, split-at splits
at one, and prepend adds elements at the front.

The verbs fall into a few families. Every one is listed with its exact
signature in the catalogue — (doc NAME) — and this section is a map of what is
there.

Positional access. first, second, third, last, rest, and nth.
These are hold-blind: on a held form (first (' a b c)) is the ' head.

Slicing. take/drop-first (the first n, the rest), take-last/
drop-last, and take-while/drop-while.

Partitioning and grouping. partition coll n (fixed-size runs),
partition-by f coll (runs where f changes), split-by f coll,
gather-by f coll, group-by f coll (a map from the printed key to the
elements), frequencies (a map from each element to its count),
distinct/dedupe/count-distinct, and shuffle.

Ordering and order statistics. sort (with key= and reverse=),
sort-by, reverse, sum, product, mean, median, variance, and
std. sort and reverse take a tensor branch: linear without dims=, shape
preserving with it. The statistics reduce a tensor along dims= and take
drop=.

Set-like verbs. union, intersect, difference, subset?, and
superset?.

Combining. zip (element-wise tuples), zipmap (a map from one sequence
to another), interleave, map-thread (f applied across several collections,
stopping at the shortest), outer (the outer product, nested one level per
collection), riffle (a separator between elements), tuples, flatten,
transpose, and subdivide.

Constructing. range ((range n), (range start stop),
(range start step stop)), repeat, and array ((array f n) builds a
sequence by calling f on 0 … n-1).

Transforming the map. keys, vals, invert, map-keys (the function
receives a keyword and must return a symbol), and deep-map (bottom-up over
every node).

The higher-order verbs take a function: a symbol naming a rule, a
replacement rule in head position ((?x -> …)), or a partial application
((part f a)). See 

Lambdas.(map (?x -> (* 2 x)) (1 2 3))         # => (2 4 6)
(filter (?x \ even?) (1 2 3 4))       # => (2 4)
(remove (?x \ even?) (1 2 3 4))       # => (1 3)
(reduce + 0 (1 2 3 4))                # => 10     (fold is a synonym)
(mapcat (?x -> (repeat 2 x)) (1 2))    # => (1 1 2 2)
(each println (1 2 3))                # prints three lines, returns naught
(apply + (1 2 3))                     # => 6
(any? even? (1 3 4))                  # => true
(all? even? (2 4))                    # => true
(none? even? (1 3))                   # => true
(sort-by (?x -> x.age) people)        # a copy, ascending by age

map defaults to depth=1 (the collection’s elements); depth=0 applies the
function to the collection itself, and depth=n rebuilds the structure around
the nodes at that level. map on a table maps rows; on a tensor it maps
elements. filter filters rows of a table.

memoize wraps a function in a process-local cache keyed by its arguments
(memoized is the internal form); a def can also be memoized directly with
memoize=true, which is described in 

Patterns.

thread distributes a form over its sequential container elements,
Mathematica-style. The head is not special and a nested hold is an ordinary
form:(thread (f (1 2 3)))          # => ((f 1) (f 2) (f 3))
(hold-thread (' f (1 2 3)))   # => (' (f 1) (f 2) (f 3))
(thread (' f (1 2 3)))        # => ((' f 1) (' f 2) (' f 3))

hold-thread strips the argument’s root hold before threading and holds the
result; hold= selects the result’s heldness (false on thread, true on
hold-thread).

The pipeline >> substitutes a value into raw step forms and reduces only
the final form. _ is the placeholder:(let (x=2) (x >> (_ + 1) (f _) (result=_)))   # => (result=(f 3))
(1 >> (_ + _) (' _))                          # => (' (1 + 1)), not '2

Evaluate x, substitute its result textually for every _ in the raw first
step, substitute that form into the next step, and so on; a step with no _
raises. (>> x step…) is the prefix spelling.

replace, rreplace, map, cases, and drop-cases accept depth=n,
selecting the level they operate on. depth=0 is the subject itself; depth=n
is every node n element steps down, where both sequence elements and map
values are children, with the structure above rebuilt. A scalar is its own sole
element, so descending past a scalar stays on it; an extern is opaque.
replace and rreplace default to depth=0; map, cases, and drop-cases
default to depth=1:(replace ((a 1) (a 2)) ((a ?x) -> x))          # => ((a 1) (a 2))  (depth 0)
(replace ((a 1) (a 2)) ((a ?x) -> x) depth=1)  # => (1 2)
(map (?x -> (wrap x)) (a=(1 2) b=3) depth=2)
# => (a=((wrap 1) (wrap 2)) b=(wrap 3))

replace-all and rreplace-all keep their whole-tree walk when depth is
absent; with depth=n they operate only on level n (so depth=0 is then
exactly replace). cases collects the elements at a level that match a
clause, and drop-cases removes them; matches-any? asks the same question
over the whole tree. The clause grammar — a bare pattern, a rule-level \
guard, or a replacement rule — is the pattern language of


Patterns.

where reports where a value occurs:(where (:a :b :b :c) :b)                # => (2 3)   the bare keys
(where ((1 2) (3 2)) 2 depth=2)         # => ((1 2) (2 2))   one path each
(where (:a :b (:a :b) :c) :b depth=:all)  # => ((2) (3 2))

With no depth it searches depth 1 and returns the bare keys of the
matches in encounter order; with an explicit non-negative integer depth it
returns one path per occurrence, each path a list of d keys. At
depth=0 the only key is the whole-form key 0, so the result is ((0)) when
the subject equals obj and () otherwise. depth=:all searches every depth
and returns one path per occurrence, each of its own length. No match is ()
in every mode, results are plain (not held), and a path splices into get,
with, or update-in.

Patterns — the pattern language and the traversal clause forms.

Tables and 

Tensors — their own path grammars.

Data model — holds, equality, and the form itself.

Mutability — set! and swap! for a mutable inside a form.

Air has four values for work that is not simply a reduction: a task runs a
body on another Julia task; a promise carries a value from one task to
another; a delay computes a body at most once; and an actor applies
functions to a value sequentially. All four are database-backed, so they survive
a serialization round trip and a process restart. Streams
(

Streams), scheduled events (

Events), and agent
sessions (

Agents) are built on the same idea.

(task form…) holds its arguments and evaluates them on a separate task,
returning a database-backed promise immediately. (await p) blocks until
the task finishes and returns the value of the final form, or rethrows the
task’s error; (get p) and (ready? p) read the same promise.

A task captures its enclosing lexical scope (like a closure), keeps the
namespace context active at the point it was created, and inherits the
current task’s val bindings:(val x 10)
(bind (x=100) (await (task (+ x 1))))   # => 101

The spawned task receives a copy of the bindings, so a later bind in the
parent does not change what the task sees. bindings=false installs no
overrides and bindings=(x=1 …) installs exactly those values. A clean=true
option clears .env and the bindings; an explicit bindings= wins over it.

Because a form is data, (task (' a b)) delivers the held form (' a b)
rather than evaluating it. An (exit v) inside a task delivers v.

A task is a process item: its promise lives in the current namespace’s
database, but the running task itself is not serialized, so a promise whose
task never delivered (because the process stopped) is simply never delivered.
(task form… durable=true name=:x) instead registers a durable task — a
record in $.config.tasks that reruns from the start after a restart,
replaying its (checkpoint form) steps — and (do-at …), (do-in …),
(tx-at …), and (tx-in …) schedule events the same way. See


Events and Durable Tasks.

(promise) is a single-assignment value in the current namespace’s database.
(deliver p v) fills it once, (get p)/(await p) read it — blocking until
it is delivered, except inside a transaction, which raises instead — and
(ready? p) tests it. A promise serializes as a link ("~uuid") whether it is
pending or delivered, and stores a row either way, so a reader of the stored
form waits on the same promise rather than on a copy of its value. task
returns such a promise; deliver and await also accept an ephemeral promise
extern. promise? tests one.

(delay body…) computes its body lazily and at most once. (get d),
(get d 0), and any get path that walks through d force it; a delay
vanishes on the path exactly as a mutable does. Free lexical names are
substituted into the body like a task’s, and the namespace context active at
creation — the current namespace, its active using layers, the thread-local
val bindings, @, and .env — is saved with it, so the body runs correctly
later, even after the database is reopened. The first force stores the value in
the delay’s database cell and every later force returns it without running the
body again:(val counter (mut 0))
(val d (delay (set! counter (+ (get counter) 1))))
(get d)        # => 1
(get d)        # => 1 (the body does not run again)
(get counter)  # => 1

A delay is immutable and never forces on printing or serialization. The body
runs as the user who forces it (like a stored def), and a body that forces its
own delay raises a catchable error rather than recursing. delay? tests one.

(actor value history=true) is a sequential worker whose value is persisted on
every update. (send a fn) sends the function fn (which receives the current
value and returns the new one) and (reset! a value) replaces the value
directly; both are deferred to commit inside a transaction, and (sync) flushes
a pending send.

The send closes over the caller’s lexical scope the way a task does: a
loop/for binding or rule parameter used inside fn is substituted with its
value, and the namespace context active at the call (its using layers and
val bindings) is kept, so a rule name or a val still resolves. A name bound
by the function’s own pattern shadows the captured one, so
(for (x …) (send a (?x -> …))) uses the parameter, not the loop’s x.
actor? tests one.

A val is an Air Var whose current value lives in per-Julia-task storage; a
bind overlays that storage for a dynamic extent. A spawned task inherits a
snapshot of the overrides, not the Var itself, which is why a later bind in
the parent does not change a running task. (bindings) renders the overrides
as a plain mapping and bind can reinstall one; see


Thread-local values.
An event or durable job can capture the same mapping as data, so it sees
the values as of creation rather than as of firing; see


Events and Durable Tasks.

A task, delay, actor, or promise belongs to the database of the namespace where
it was created, and storing one in another database raises
(error :un-storable target). An error raised by a task body is delivered to
await and rethrown there, so (do (await (task (raise :boom))) (except ?e :caught)) is :caught. Catch scopes and handler scopes are task-local and do
not cross a (task …) boundary: a notify in a task with no local handler is
an :unhandled-signal error, and an unmatched throw becomes an
:uncaught-throw error rethrown by await. A durable task or event delivers
its error as a value instead, so (await p) returns (error …).

The previous chapters described the form and how it reduces. This chapter
describes the forms that decide what runs: conditionals, boolean logic,
binding, loops, and sequencing. Pattern dispatch (case), traversal, and the
higher-order collection verbs build on the pattern language and are covered in


Patterns and 

Collections; the block form’s
error and signal clauses are covered in 

Errors and blocks.

Two values are false and one kind of form is false:

false;

naught (and therefore the empty form ()); and

an empty container.

Everything else is true — including 0, the empty string "", and the keyword
:false. Predicates such as zero?, empty?, and naught? are the explicit
tests; a condition written in a conditional or a when is interpreted by this
rule.

if takes alternating conditions and values, with an optional trailing else
value:(if (< n 2) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1))))
(if (< x 0) :negative (== x 0) :zero :positive)
(if ready :go)                      # => naught when ready is false

The conditions are evaluated in order and the value paired with the first
truthy one is selected; that value is then reduced in tail position (see
below). Extra condition/value pairs are the else-if chain — the form above
reads “if x < 0 then :negative, else if x == 0 then :zero, else
:positive”. With no true condition and no else value the result is naught.
cond is a synonym.

Comparison is ==, !=, <, <=, >, or >=; a single = only separates
a map key from its value, so (= x 0) is not a comparison.

when evaluates its body when the condition is true and yields the last body
value; otherwise it is naught. unless is the negation:(when (empty? coll) (println "nothing to do"))
(unless (empty? coll) (process coll))

Both take any number of body forms and sequence them like a do with no
clauses.

and and or are the short-circuiting operators. and yields the last value
when every argument is true and the first false value otherwise; or yields
the first true value and the last value otherwise. The empty cases are (and)
→ true and (or) → naught. not is prefix-only, and xor is true when an
odd number of its arguments are true:(and (< 0 n) (< n 10))              # n is in range
(or fallback (compute))             # compute only when fallback is false
(not ready)
(xor a b)                           # exactly one of a and b

and/or are operators, not functions: (a and b) is (and a b), and they
may be used infix. There is no (a and not b) reader form — write
(a and (not b)).

let takes a binding form as its second element, followed by a body:(let (x=1 y=2) (+ x y))       # => 3

The bindings in one mapping are parallel: every value is evaluated in the
enclosing scope, before any of the names is substituted. let then substitutes
each name by its value in the body textually, before the body is evaluated, so
it does not introduce a scope of its own — it rewrites the body. Substitution
reaches every occurrence, including occurrences inside a quoted form:(let (x=2) (' a x b))                    # => (' a 2 b)
(let (y=10) (let (x=y) (?y -> x)))        # => (?y -> 10)

The binding form may also be a sequence of mappings, each of which feeds the
next: names bound by earlier groups are substituted into later groups’ value
expressions before those are evaluated. Within a group the bindings stay
parallel, and a rebound name refers to its previous value inside its own new
value:(let ((a=1 b=2) (c=(a + b))) c)          # => 3
(let ((x=1) (x=(x + 2))) x)              # => 3

A hold=(x y) option on the let form names bindings whose values are inserted
exactly as written instead of evaluated (in every group; earlier groups still
substitute into them):(def (hold-y y=?y ??rest) hold=y)
(let (x=(1 + 1) y=(2 + 2) z=(3 + 3)) hold=(y z) (hold-y x=x y=y z=z))
# => (hold-y x=2 y=(2 + 2) z=6)

(let ((a=1 b=2) (c=(a + b))) hold=c (hold c))   # => (' (1 + 2))

A bind=(x y) option names bindings that are bound, not substituted: each
value is evaluated and installed as a lexical name instead of being written into
the body. Bound and substituted names live side by side, so a substituted value
may mention a bound name and resolves against it. The option goes on the let
form, or on a sequence binding form’s own map (where a :let marker must put it):(let ((const=2.551 f=((a ^ 2) / ((a + b) ^ 2)))
      (a=(2 * const) b=(4 * (const ^ 2))) hold=f bind=(a b))
  f)                                     # => 0.02685688214587777

(do :let ((a=1) (b=(a + 1)) bind=(a b)) (+ a b))   # => 3

const substitutes into a and b; a and b are bound; hold=f inserts
f’s expression, which then evaluates against the bound a and b. A name
cannot be both held and bound. let= (used by blocks) already binds every name
and takes neither option.

Because a value is inserted rather than looked up, a value whose head is its own
name is harmless: (let (db=(db 1)) db) is (db 1).

The body of a let is a sequence of forms; it yields the last value. A let
body is in tail position, and a let body is also a lexical scope for loop
and for bindings made inside it.

loop binds names, evaluates a body, and re-enters the loop when the body
reaches a recur:(loop (i 1 acc 0)
  (if (> i 10) acc (recur (i + 1) (acc + i))))    # => 55

recur supplies the new values for the loop’s names, in order. In tail
position it re-enters the loop in constant stack; a recur that is not in
tail position is still control flow but is not optimized. recur is not an
error: no except clause catches it. A loop with no recur simply yields its
body’s value.

while repeats its body while a condition stays true and yields naught:(let (m=(mut 0))
  (while (< (get m) 3) (set! m (+ (get m) 1)))
  (get m))                                  # => 3

(mut and set! are described in 

Mutability.)

for is a comprehension. Its binding form names a sequence of collection/name
pairs, processed left to right and nested, with :if cond and :let name val
steps in between. The result is the list of body values (range builds a
sequence of numbers; see 

Collections):(for (x (range 1 4)) (* x 2))                    # => (2 4 6)
(for (x (range 1 6) :if (even? x)) x)            # => (2 4)
(for (r rows :let (n=(get r :name))) n)          # one value per row

The table chapter shows for over rows; a tensor iterates linearly in
column-major order (see 

Tensors). doseq is the same binding form
for effect and returns naught; dotimes binds a counter to 0 … n-1 and also
returns naught. each (in 

Collections) is the same idea for
a function over a collection.

do evaluates its body forms left to right and yields the last value. It is the
general block form: it also takes let= (a lexical scope around the whole block),
:let markers inside the body (nested textual lets), catch= for throw,
and trailing except, handle, and finally clauses. The full grammar, the
clause semantics, and throw/signal are in 

Errors and blocks.

A def body and a val body are the same block: several forms are sequenced as
a do, and the block options and clauses apply. A body that needs none of them
is stored exactly as written. See 

Definition bodies.

Reduction runs bottom-up to a fixed point. A call in tail position is
reduced iteratively rather than recursively, so a tail-recursive rule runs in
constant stack; only nested (non-tail) recursion is bounded by the depth budget.
Tail positions are:

the selected branch of an if/cond;

the last form of a let or loop body, or of a do with no
catch=/except/handle/finally (with or without :let/let=);

the body of when/unless;

the last operand of and/or; and

a rule body — a def body, a lambda’s replacement, or a case clause (see


Patterns).

tx is never a tail form.

(exit [value]) ends the current task — the REPL, a loaded file, a task
body, or an SSH session turns it into that boundary’s result — so a plain
air_eval sees it propagate. It is control flow, not an error, so no error
clause catches it. With no value it is naught.

Patterns — def, wildcards, case, and pattern dispatch.

Collections — map, filter, reduce, thread,
pipelines, and traversal.

Errors and blocks — except, catch/throw, handle, and
finally.

Mutability — set!, filters and watches, tx, sandbox.

Every value in air is a form: an immutable, JSON-like tree of scalars and
containers. Code is a form too, which is why a rule can rewrite a program and a
program can build a rule. This chapter describes the form itself, quoted forms
(holds), and the three equality relations. Mutable state is the one exception to
immutability and is described in 

Mutability and
transactions; the accessor and update verbs are in


Collections.

A form is an immutable object that contains actual data. Strings, symbols,
numbers (see 

Numbers for the eight numeric leaves),
booleans, and the null value naught are all considered subtypes of the
form type.

Collections: Sequences (whitespace-separated elements surrounded by
parentheses) and mappings (paired values with keys, e.g., (a=1 b=2 c=3))
are forms.

Hybrid Forms: Forms can include both sequential and mapping values: (f 1 2 a=3 b=4) is a form with three sequential elements and two mapping
elements. Keyword elements do not need to come in any particular order, and
their ordering is not preserved ((f 1 2 a=3 b=4), (a=3 b=4 f 1 2), and
(f a=3 1 b=4 2) are all equal forms).

Empty Form: There is exactly one empty form (), which is considered
logically false and identical to naught (acting as a nil value).

Querying and updating: a form can be indexed by treating it as a
function — for a form f equal to (1 (2 3) a=(g h i)), (f 1) returns
1, (f 2) returns (2 3), and (f :a) returns (g h i) — and get,
with, wout, update, update-in, push, and pop are the verbs behind
that idea. A path is a sequence of keys, an integer key counts from 1, and a
missing key is naught to update-in’s function. 

Collections
covers the accessor, the lone-: wildcard, the scalar-as-singleton
convention, locating with where, and the whole collection surface.

A scalar is its own sole sequence for the accessors: (get 10 1) is 10,
descending past a scalar stays on it, and out-of-bounds indices throw, so a
scalar participates naturally in collection operations ((push 10 11) is
(10 11)). This is an accessor convention, not a rewrite: a written
container is never collapsed, so 10, (10), and ((10)) are three distinct
forms and (eq? 10 (10)) is false. A one-element form reduces only when a
def (or builtin) matches it. The sole canonicalization is the empty form:
() and naught are the same singleton at every depth, so (same? () naught)
is true and no container ever embeds an empty container.

Holding is structural, not a flag: the canonical hold is a container whose
first element is the ordinary symbol ', (' a b c). ' is an ordinary
symbol character (a'b is a symbol), but a symbol may not begin with it —
except the bare ' itself. There is no separate held bit on a form, and a held
form is an ordinary value everywhere. 'x is reader sugar for (' x) when x
is a scalar ('a, '5, ':x, '"abc"); the container spelling '(…) is
a parse error — write (' …).

Literal Forms: a hold holds each of its elements as written, so
(' a b c) holds three elements and (' (a b c)) holds one container. '5
and ':a stay held as well. A hold of exactly one scalar prints with the
quote ('a, '5, ':a); any other hold prints literally ((' a b c),
(' f x=1)). (hold e…) is the reserved alias that reduces to (' e…).
A held form does not reduce — it is data. (unhold (' a b c)) drops the head
and evaluates the remaining content, giving (a b c).

Unquoting (~): ~e is sugar for (preval e), a reserved special form
that evaluates e eagerly wherever it appears. Inside a held form each
~e is filled in with the reduced form of e at every depth (a nested hold
fills its own holes): (hold (a ~(1 + 2))) reduces to (' (a 3)). ~ is
not the runtime unhold operation — that is the ordinary call (unhold x),
which evaluates a held form’s content. Use lift (below) to build a quoted
form explicitly from literal and evaluated parts. A hole may be a map value
((f x=~(1 + 2)) is (f x=3), and x=~y is the same hole in atom form),
and a trailing ... splices the hole’s value into the enclosing sequence
rather than its operand ((f ~(1 2 3)...) is (f 1 2 3)).

Access: because a hold is an ordinary form, the hold-blind accessors see it
as one — (first (' a b c)) is ' and (count (' a b c)) is 4. get
indexes the form as written, so for a held form index 1 is the ' head and
index 2 is the first element of its content: (get (' f a b) 2) is f and
(get (' f x=1) :x) is 1. Pass hold=true to make the root hold
transparent — the path then indexes the content, intermediate values are not
reduced, and the result is held: (get (' f (1 + 2)) 2 hold=true) is
(' 1 + 2). This works for any form that keeps its arguments as data
((get (part add 10) 2 hold=true) is 'add, where part is the partial
application of 

Patterns).
(with form k1 v1 … hold=true) is the inverse: it replaces the subform at
each path with its value, inserted without its own hold and not evaluated —
(with (' a b c) 2 (' 1 + 1) hold=true) is (' a (1 + 1) c). (held? x)
tests whether x is a held form, and (held? form k…) tests the subpart at
that path (hold=true makes the root hold transparent first). lower pushes
holds toward the leaves and lift lifts them back to the root
((lift (' ' a x ' b)) → (' a <value-of-x> b)).

The hold- family: every collection operation that takes a primary form
has a hold- version — hold-get, hold-nth, hold-with, hold-wout,
hold-push, hold-push-in, hold-join, hold-join-in, hold-update,
hold-thread, hold-held?. These treat the primary form’s root hold as
transparent (the operation is on the content), let inserted held values
contribute their content, and return the result held:
(hold-get (' 1 2 3) 2) is (' 2). Each takes hold= to select the result’s
heldness ((hold-get (' 1 2 3) 2 hold=false) is 2), and the plain version
accepts hold=true for the same treatment ((get (1 2 3) 2 hold=true) is
(' 2)).

Three relations are distinct:

(same? a b) is object identity (===).

(eq? a b) is equivalence. Two scalars are equivalent when they have the
same value and the same type, so (eq? 1 1.0) is false even though
(== 1 1.0) is true. A signed zero is one value under equivalence
((eq? -0.0 0.0) is true) and NaN is equivalent to itself. Two containers
are equivalent when their sequences are
elementwise equivalent and their maps hold equivalent values under the same
keys (map order is irrelevant). A mutable — a shared, writable cell,
described in 

Mutability — and the database-backed handles
(an actor, a promise) are equivalent only to themselves; an extern follows its own
isequal, so two separately compiled equal regex values are equivalent while
two tasks’ promises are not. A delay is equivalent when its type and its
serialization agree — equivalence never forces one. Everything immutable
is therefore comparable by
value, even when it points at a mutable: the mutable part contributes only
its identity.

(== a b) is content equality, the numeric-friendly relation used by the
arithmetic comparisons ((== 1 1.0) is true, as are (== -0.0 0.0) and
(== (f 1) (f 1.0))). It is AirDB’s ==, under which a NaN is equal to
nothing, just as in Julia; eq? is the relation that treats NaN as equal to
itself.

(hash x) follows eq?: equivalent forms hash alike, and the hash never
descends into a mutable object (a volatile hashes by its identity), so any
immutable form is hashable even when it contains one. Two forms that hash alike
need not be equivalent, but equivalent forms always hash alike, which is what a
memoization table or a keyed map needs.

A process starts with one private in-memory database holding the air root
(.air, .sys, .lib, .main, and the system user records). (open-airdb name opts…) opens an AirDB database, roots a namespace at name in it, and
attaches @ to that root for the calling task. From Julia, Env(db = d) selects
the process database — the store behind ., .main, and a system user’s
home — and does not change the database of any opened root:(open-airdb .work memory=true)      ; an in-memory database (as in the tests)
(open-airdb .work dbname="air" user="air" host="localhost" port=5432)
(open-airdb .work url="postgresql://air@localhost/air" create=true)

option

meaning

memory=true

a fresh in-memory database

url= / conninfo=

a libpq connection string, passed through verbatim

dbname= user= host= port= password= sslmode=

a PostgreSQL connection (host defaults to localhost, port to 5432)

create=true

create the schema (create_database); the PostgreSQL database itself must exist

create=false

open an existing schema only

(absent)

try to open, then create

A bare name is relative to the current namespace (so air’s (open-airdb work …) roots .main.work); an explicit .path or @.path is absolute.
Opening requires write on the containing namespace, and a root may not be
placed over an existing namespace or where a database is already open. Unless
the opener is air, opening writes the opener’s user record into the database;
an admin’s status carries over. A newly created root is owned by its opener.

A namespace at or under an opened root lives in that database (the
longest-prefixed open root wins), so (namespace .work.util …) is durable
there. @ addresses the same root: with .work open, @.util.f is
.work.util.f. Opening a database inside another ((open-airdb .work.sub …))
creates a distinct database that owns the namespaces at or under .work.sub,
with its own users and permissions.

Database users are separate from system users. (create-user :bob) while
attached writes @.user.bob into the attached database; (users) lists that
database’s users (air included); and a permission map in a database may name
only one of its own users (or _), so (chmod! .work read=(mallory=true))
raises a bad-user error. A user of another database is likewise not a valid
principal.

Because namespaces in a database are persisted as linked volatiles, a value
assigned there must be storable: it may not embed a volatile from another
database. Storing .main’s mutable or the .air namespace raises
(error :un-storable target) instead of writing an unresolvable link. mut inside a
database namespace creates its mutable in that same database.

(close-airdb name) flushes and closes the database, removes its root namespace
from the parent, and detaches @ (returning it to .) when it pointed at that
root. Closing a database also closes any database rooted beneath it. From Julia,
open_airdb!(env, path, db) roots an already-opened database — the way the
tests use MemoryDatabase — and close_airdb!(env, path) closes it.

The process database also holds .sys.ssh.<key> for every SSH server that has
been started under that name: private and public vals holding the host key
and a config mapping recording the owner and key type. .sys is readable only
by air, so the record is reached through the SSH builtins
((ssh-host-key key)), never by a path; it is what makes a reopened server the
same host. See 

SSH access.

A form’s database is the database of the namespace it is written in, never
an ambient store chosen by the environment. The system namespaces (., .air,
.sys, .lib, .main, and a system user’s home) live in the process database;
a namespace at or under an opened root lives in that root’s database. mut,
logic-set, the named-form operations, form-at, and from-json all follow
this one rule, so a mutable made in .main belongs to the process store even
while @ points elsewhere, and storing it in a database namespace raises
(error :un-storable …).

AirDB registers a name for a volatile, giving a form a durable, database-wide
handle:(named-form :counter create=true value=3)   ; create and name a new volatile
(named-form :counter)                       ; the same volatile
(value (named-form :counter))               ; 3
(named-form :counter create=false)          ; raises when the name is absent
(named-form :counter create=naught)         ; naught when the name is absent
(named-form :alias create=true value=(named-form :counter))  ; an alias
(name-form! :other (named-form :counter))   ; repoint an existing name
(named-forms)                               ; (alias=(mut 3) counter=(mut 3) …)

A name may be a keyword, a raw symbol, or a string; :counter and "counter"
agree, and the leading colon of a keyword is stripped, so (named-form :counter) registers counter. Names beginning air/ are reserved for air’s
own bookkeeping and neither appear in named-forms nor may be created.
value= may be an ordinary form or an existing volatile of the same database,
in which case the name becomes an alias for it (no new form is made). A
created form records its history unless history=false. The name table is
transactional: a creation or repointing joins the enclosing transaction, so it
is retried or discarded with it, and a failed transaction leaves no name behind.

Creating a name publishes an entry from the current namespace, so it needs
write there (and a user record in a database); a lookup needs read on the
named form. A new named form is owned by its creator with the default owner-only
ACL. named-forms lists the names the caller may read. name-form! may claim a
free name with write in the namespace; repointing an existing name instead
needs write on the form currently named (or on the database root, for a
database administrator).

Every namespace is implicitly a logic set, so the facts and rules asserted
into it are stored as the hidden named form air/logic/<path> (air/logic at
the root) in the namespace’s own database. They therefore persist with that
database, share the namespace’s access control, and never appear in
named-forms; air/ is reserved, so the set cannot be opened by name. The set
is created lazily by the first fact or rule write, a namespace with no set
reads as an empty set, and a read never creates one.(namespace .app)
(assert .app (depends :app :lib1))       ; creates air/logic/app
(facts .app)                             ; => (' (depends :app :lib1))

(logic-set :s) makes a standalone set instead, an ordinary named form
whose value has the logic-set shape; the two differ only in how their
permissions are mapped. 

Production rules
describes both targets, the operations, their results, and their permissions.

(sync) blocks until every write committed before the call has reached the
database; (sync target) targets a namespace or volatile instead of the current
namespace’s database. It is a barrier, not a drain: it queues a flush behind
the writes already scheduled, so writes that other tasks schedule afterward do
not delay it, and the sequential writer cannot be starved by continuing
activity. (status) returns (pending=N error=naught): the number of updates
scheduled but not yet written, and the last writer error. Both are also
.air.sys.sync and .air.sys.status.

Air defers an actor message sent inside an open transaction until that
transaction commits, so a sync placed inside a namespace, load-air, or
other transaction cannot include that transaction’s own writes. It flushes
every write already scheduled and returns; the block’s writes are scheduled when
the block commits, so call (sync) outside the block to make them durable. A
MemoryDatabase has nothing to flush, so its sync returns at once.

(form-id volatile) returns the form’s UUID as a string. (form-at id) returns
the volatile with that id in the current database without loading its body; when
no such form is in the database, reading the handle raises (error :form-not-found id). (loaded? volatile) reports whether the body has been read into memory,
and (history volatile) whether the form records its history.

(to-json value) encodes a form as JSON text and (from-json text) decodes it
in the current database. The codec is AirDB’s: numbers and booleans are JSON
scalars, naught is null, a string is a JSON string carrying its reader quote
('hi), a keyword is a JSON string carrying its colon ("::x"), a form is the
pair [sequence, map], and a volatile is the link string "@uuid". Links are
never expanded, so a cyclic structure encodes; from-json resolves each link
through the current database, and a link to a missing form raises
(error :form-not-found id). An extern encodes by type and id ({"extern": …, "id": …}) and reads back through the database’s resource registry. The
database reference forms have their own encodings: an actor is "!uuid", a
promise is "~uuid" until it is delivered (then it encodes as its value), and a
delay is {"delay": ":air", "form": <the cell's link>} — never forced by
encoding. A form bound for a database may embed only volatiles, actors, promises,
and delays of that same database; anything else raises
(error :un-storable target).

Printing is cycle-safe on the same terms: a volatile that contains itself prints
the inner occurrence opaquely as #<volatile uuid> instead of recursing.

JSON has no infinity or NaN, so AirDB writes a non-finite float as a marked
string: Inf is "#inf", -Inf is "#-inf", and NaN is "#nan". The #
marker cannot be confused with a string ('), a symbol (:), or a link (@),
and a literal string that looks like one is still a string, so (to-json inf)
is the JSON string "#inf" while (to-json "#inf") is "'#inf". Such a value
flushes to any database, including the .air constants inf and nan.

The rest of the numeric tower has a marker too, so an exact value never degrades
on the way through JSON: a BigInt is "#big:…", a rational "#rat:n/d" (or
"#bigrat:n/d"), and a BigFloat "#bigfloat:<bits>:…". See


Numbers.

Air documents itself. Every builtin and operator — 576 builtins and 17
operators, plus the reserved heads error, signal, and ui — has an entry
in a process-global catalogue, so nothing in the language is reachable only
through an external manual. The catalogue, the air-level docstrings on your own
defs, and the namespace listings are all ordinary air values, so a REPL
session, an agent, and this book read the same source.

(help) prints an introduction to the language: the form, evaluation, holds,
namespaces, and errors in a page, ending with a list of things to try next.

(doc) and (doc .air) return the index — every documented name grouped by
category, with a count per category. (doc NAME) returns one entry: the name,
its category as (builtin :collection), and the catalogue text. (doc .air.NAME)
is the same lookup through the core namespace, and .air.NAME also names any of
them as a callable: (.air.sqrt 9) is 3.0.

(doc NAME) (and (doc .air.NAME)) then lists the documented def rules that
use the name, newest first, each with its docstring. (doc (form…)) holds its
argument rather than evaluating it and lists the documented rules whose patterns
match that form, which is how you find out which definition handles
(doc (log 1.0)):(doc .air.sqrt)     # the builtin entry
(doc log)           # the builtin (if any) plus every documented rule using log
(doc (log 1.0))     # only the rules that match that call

(help NAME) prints exactly the text (doc NAME) returns; (help :category)
prints one category’s name list, and (help :all) prints the whole index.
Both write through the environment’s output stream, so a session over SSH
prints to that client.

A literal string at the head of a def body is the rule’s docstring. It is
removed from the executable body, deindented, and recorded with the definition
in its namespace, so it survives a reload and a restart. The same doc/help
machinery reads it; 

Patterns describes the
placement rules.

(definitions arg) takes the same argument as (doc …) but returns the
matching def forms as held data instead of text. Each docstring moves from the
head of the body into a doc= map entry, and a hold= or memoize= option is
reproduced:(definitions log)
# => ((' def (log ?x \ number?) ... doc="Returns the natural log of x.") …)

Because the forms are quoted data, a body that needs to unhold at run time uses
(unhold x) rather than ~ — see the note at the end of


Docstrings.

The catalogue is air source: src/core.air holds one (docdef CATEGORY name… "text"…) form per name, or per family of names that share a description. It is
read into BUILTIN_DOCS when the package loads, so changing it invalidates the
image rather than requiring a rebuild of the documentation.

The optional first element is the category; it names the index group.

The names are raw symbols, or a form of them, so a family documents together.

The trailing strings are joined and deindented into one text.

Registration semantics. A docdef is a registration like layout, not a
definition: it is process-global, neither scoped nor transactional, and
sandbox does not undo one. The first entry for a name fixes its category and
its place in the index; a later docdef amends it, appending its text as a
further paragraph. That is how a specialized entry can extend a general one —
the get entry for a tensor path follows the general get entry rather than
replacing it. A library can document the names it adds the same way, which is
why core.air is ordinary air source rather than a Julia table.

A docdef accepts the reserved heads (error, signal, ui, and any builtin)
precisely because it documents a name rather than defining one; a def could
not define them.

The builtin catalogue covers what ships with the language. The definitions in a
namespace are listed by the namespace forms, all of which default to the current
namespace and filter by permission — an entry the caller may not read is
absent, exactly as in using and doc:

returns

Air features a pattern-matched, structural error system integrated directly into
its core evaluation engine, replacing traditional class-based exception
hierarchies. Errors are ordinary forms, so they can be stored, matched, compared,
and printed like any other value.

An error object is a form whose first element is the ordinary symbol
error:(error :io "Connection lost")
(error)                    # the empty error
(error :arg :a x=1)        # the map is part of the object

The reducer never evaluates an error object or any of its elements: error is
an inert head, so (error :io (+ 1 2)) is the unevaluated form
(error :io (+ 1 2)) at any depth. The first element after the head is
conventionally the error type (a keyword), but air never inspects it; the type
is optional and purely conventional. error cannot be given a reduction rule.

raise is a special form that constructs an error object and throws it.(raise :io "Connection lost" path="/tmp/x")

Arguments are evaluated. (raise :io (+ 1 2)) raises
(error :io 3). Map entries are evaluated too.

No type is required. (raise), (raise :io), and (raise "oops") are
all legal; they raise (error), (error :io), and (error "oops").

The first slot is not special. (raise :io "x") raises (error :io "x")
and (raise "a" "b") raises (error "a" "b").

A single error object is raised exactly. If raise has exactly one
positional argument and no options and that argument evaluates to an
(error …) object, the object is thrown as it is — its elements are not
re-evaluated or copied:(raise (error :io (+ 1 2)))        # throws (error :io (+ 1 2))
(raise (error :io) "abc")          # (error (error :io) "abc")

Adding any option (or a second argument) makes raise rebuild an object, so
the error object becomes the first payload element.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally
3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
do is the language’s block form and subsumes the old try: it evaluates a
body with optional binding, error clauses, signal handlers, and a finalizer.
tx accepts exactly the same grammar and runs it inside one transaction.(do
    let=(scale=2)                       # a lexical block scope
    :let (x=(compute scale))            # a textual binding inside the body
    (some-function x)                   # body…
  (except (:io ??data)                  # matches the content of (error :io …)
    (print "I/O failed: " data)
    :handled)
  (except (:arg ?x \ symbol?)
    :bad-argument)
  (except ?err                          # a bare wildcard binds the whole object
    (print "Unrecognized error: " err)
    reraise)                            # resume it (see below)
  (handle (:progress ?pct)              # a notified signal runs here and
    (print pct "%"))                    # execution continues after notify
  (finally
    (print "done")))

A block is(do options… body… (except pattern body…)… (handle pattern body…)… (finally body…)?)

The only options are let= and catch=. The body runs left to right, and the
clauses that follow it may be except and handle in any order; at most one
finally may appear, and it must be last. A bare (catch …) clause is an
error: write catch= for a throw tag or except for an error pattern.
except/handle outside a block remain ordinary data.

The block’s value is the last body value (naught for an empty body), a caught
throw value, or the matching except/handle body’s value. finally’s value
is discarded. Block setup — the let= values and the catch= tags — runs
before the body; a failure there is not handled by the same block’s clauses and
does not run its finally (an outer block can still handle it).

hierarchy.lvl2: 3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally
3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
A level-1 bare :let in the body consumes the next body form as a let
binding form; the remaining body forms become its body. Markers nest left to
right, need not be first, and a marker in the final body position is inert
data. :let is the same textual let as elsewhere: its names are substituted
into the rest of the body, and they are not visible to except, handle,
or finally.

let= instead wraps the whole block in one lexical scope, visible in the
body, clause bodies, signal handlers, and finally, and outermost relative to
any :let markers. Its groups feed one another exactly as let’s do, but as a
scope it does not rewrite inside a hold or a computed key.(do let=(a=1) :let (a=2) a)        ; => 2
(do let=(a=5) :let (a=2) (raise :x) (except (:x) a))   ; => 5

3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
Content matching. An except pattern is matched against the content
of the error object: the object without its error head, keeping its map.
(except (:io ?msg) …) therefore matches (error :io "x") with
msg = "x", and (except () …) matches (error).

Bare wildcards bind the object. A pattern that is a single non-rest
wildcard (?e, ?) is matched against the whole error object, so the handler
can inspect or re-raise it. Use (except (:io ??data) …) to capture the
content’s sequence and map.

First match wins. Clauses are tested top to bottom; the first matching
clause runs and later clauses are skipped.

Escaping. If no clause matches, the error continues propagating. A new
error raised inside a handler also escapes the block; it is not offered to
later clauses.

Empty body. A matching except with no body evaluates to naught and
consumes the error.

Host exceptions. A non-air exception is matched through the error object
air builds for it ((error :internal message), or a specific head such as
:form-not-found), and is rethrown unchanged when no clause matches.

3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
reraise is a reserved bare symbol (it cannot be bound by let, def, or a
pattern). When the final value of an except body is reraise, the
original error resumes as if that clause had not fired: later clauses still get
a chance to match it, and if none handles it, it escapes the block. Side
effects performed before the reraise are kept.(do (raise :io "x")
  (except (:io ?m) reraise)      ; log here, then let the next clause see it
  (except ?e (print e)))

3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
catch= makes a throw return from the block early:(let (x=-1)
  (do catch=:tag
      (if (< x 0) (throw :tag :undef))
      (sqrt x)))                 ; => :undef

catch=true is the literal tag true; catch=:tag is one tag;
catch=(tag1 tag2…) is a list. Tags are held literals, not forms and not
patterns: a symbol is not evaluated. ~expr is the only escape and must
reduce to a scalar. Any other form is an error, as are an empty catch= and
a catch= with map entries.

(throw value) means (throw true value); (throw) is
(throw true naught); (throw tag value) uses a held or computed tag. The
value is evaluated. Extra arguments or map options are errors.

At a throw, the innermost active catch= scope with a matching tag accepts
it. A block catches only signals aimed at its own scope, so same-tag nesting
is unambiguous and other signals pass through. A throw from an except
body is caught by the same block’s catch=; one from finally is not (its
catch scope is already closed), though an outer block can still catch it.

With no matching catch, the throw is immediately the ordinary error
(error :uncaught-throw tag value), raised from the throw form’s position.
except clauses therefore never see a throw signal; they see only that
error once no catch matches.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally
3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
A signal object is a form headed by the ordinary symbol signal. Like an
error object it is a constant: it never reduces, at any depth.(signal :progress 40)

(notify data…) evaluates its positional arguments and map values. With
exactly one positional argument, no map entries, and a (signal …) value, it
dispatches that object unchanged; otherwise it dispatches the freshly built
signal. Handlers are searched from the innermost active block to the outermost,
and top to bottom within a block; the first match wins. A handler pattern
matches the signal’s content (the object without its head, keeping the map),
and a bare non-rest wildcard binds the whole signal object.

A matching handler runs at the notify site in its defining block’s scope (the
block’s let= scope, plus the pattern bindings). Its value becomes notify’s
value and execution continues. A handler is dynamically scoped but lexically
evaluated: it is registered at block entry, works for a notify written
before the handle clause, and disappears when the block exits. An error
raised by a handler follows the context in which the notify ran.

With no matching handler, notify raises (error :unhandled-signal signal)
from the notify form. (notify-or default data…) is the same, except default
is held and evaluated only when nothing matches; it is not part of the signal.(do (notify :progress 40)
  (handle (:progress ?pct) (+ pct 1)))     ; => 41
(do (notify-or :none :progress 40)
  (handle (:progress ?pct) pct))           ; => 40

Catch scopes and handler scopes are task-local and do not cross a (task …)
boundary: a notify in a task with no local handler is an :unhandled-signal
error, and an unmatched throw becomes an :uncaught-throw error rethrown by
await.

3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
finally always runs — after normal completion, after a matched except, after
a caught throw, after a reraise, and while an error or throw escapes. It may
appear without any other clause, must be last, and there may be at most one. Its
value is discarded. The block’s handle scope is still active while it runs,
but its catch=/except are closed. If it raises or throws, that condition
replaces the result or the condition already in flight, and a replaced error
becomes the new error’s automatic from (see below).

3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
A def body (and a val body, which is evaluated once at definition time) is
this same block. It takes let= and catch=, level-1 :let markers, and
trailing except/handle/finally clauses; several body forms are evaluated
in sequence as by do. Everything above applies unchanged: an error from the
body can be handled by its own except, a throw by its own catch=, and a
finally always runs. 

Patterns
describes the options themselves; this section covers their consequences for
errors and transactions.

tx=true (the only def-specific option besides memoize=) runs the whole
body as a tx instead of a do:(def (store ?x) tx=true (write-something x) (raise :disk-full))
(do (store 5) (except (:disk-full) 1))
; => 1, and the write is rolled back

(def (safe-store ?x) tx=true (write-something x) (raise :disk-full)
  (except (:disk-full) :failed))
(safe-store 5)
; => :failed, and the write commits

tx=false is the default, an ordinary block with no transaction. A memoized
body caches only a successful result; an error or throw passes through and
stores nothing.
