3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
A do with no catch=, except, handle, or finally keeps its last body
form in tail position (including when it uses :let/let=), so a tail call
through it does not grow the stack. Any condition-handling feature makes the
block run eagerly, and tx is never a tail form. See 

Tail position and
exit for the full list of tail forms.

hierarchy.lvl2: 3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally
3. Blocks: do, tx, except, catch, handle, and finally

records.content:
try has been removed. Rewrite (try body… (except …)… (finally …)) as
(do body… (except …)… (finally …)); it is a tombstone that raises an error.

Python distinguishes implicit context (__context__) from an explicitly
declared cause (__cause__); air uses the map options from= and cause=.

from is automatic context. A raise inside an except handler (or a
finally with an error in flight) records the error being handled as
from=:(do (raise :disk-full) (except (:disk-full) (raise :save-failed)))
; => (error :save-failed from=(error :disk-full))

An explicit from= overrides the automatic value, and from=naught
suppresses it. Raising an error object exactly (the single-object rule) does
not add from.

cause is explicit only. Use cause= when one error transforms another:
(raise :save-failed cause=(error :disk-full)).

Both are ordinary map entries, matchable like any other; ?* and ?? capture
them, while ?& does not.

showerror prints the chain recursively, labeling an explicit cause
direct cause: and an automatic context during handling of::air error: (error :save-failed)
  ...
direct cause:
  (error :disk-full)

The walk is depth-limited to 16 links to stop cycles.

A non-air exception raised by the host (bad index, closed file, permission
denial, parse failure, …) is presented to except as an error object too,
conventionally (error :internal message). Air conditions use their own heads
(:permission-denied, :extern-expired, :database-error, :form-not-found,
:proxy-unresolved, :un-storable), all matched through their content.(do (get (1 2) 5) (except (:internal ?msg) msg))

Error handling interacts directly with Air’s Software Transactional Memory
(Air.jl) and persistence layer (AirDB.jl). The transaction model itself —
joining rather than nesting, watch, finalizers, and sandbox — is described
in 

Mutability and transactions; this section is
the error-handling view of it.

Uncaught errors abort. An error that escapes its enclosing transaction
boundary triggers an automatic STM transaction abort and rollback,
preventing partial or corrupted state changes from committing. This is true
even when an outer block catches the error: the abort has already happened.

Caught errors commit. An error intercepted and handled inside the except
clause of a do/tx running inside the transaction does not force a
rollback, letting the transaction recover or handle validation failures
gracefully.

Throws commit first. A throw caught by a block inside the
transaction returns normally and commits. A throw that escapes the
transaction to an outer catch= is deferred: the body returns normally (so
writes are not staged as an abort), watches run as on a normal exit, the
transaction commits, and only then is the signal rethrown. If the transaction
fails and Air retries, the deferred throw from the failed attempt is
discarded and the body runs again, so the throw may never complete.

Handlers run in the transaction. A handler notified while the transaction
is open is ordinary code in that transaction: its writes are transactional
and roll back with an abort. A watch error aborts; a watch throw replaces a
pending throw (the last one wins). Exceptions raised by a finally or by
finalizers/commit are outside the deferral and abort.

A tx=true definition is a boundary. The body of such a def (or val)
is an explicit tx, so an escaping error aborts the body’s writes and an
error caught by the body’s own except, or a throw caught by its own
catch=, commits. Nested inside another transaction, it joins it rather than
opening a second boundary.

Forms are data, so a position is not part of a form; the reader records the
character span of each container it parses, and a loader (load-air, a library
init.air, or the CLI) installs that record task-locally while it evaluates the
forms. Positions are best-effort: an environment that evaluates a bare form — a
REPL call, a test — has no source record and reports no position.

Two decorations are attached to an error as frames, innermost first:

The top-level form during whose evaluation the error escaped, from the
loader’s span record.

The definition site of the def whose body was executing, from the
src= entry that def/val store in the namespace entry’s body (the body is
gated by read like any other; diagnostics read it internally). The innermost
rule context wins, so an error inside g’s body reported while f calls g
describes g’s definition, not f’s.

A frame is the map form (name=… line=… col=… text=…), where name is the file
path (or <interactive>), line/col are 1-based, and text is the exact
source text of the form. showerror prints the innermost frame as
(at name:line:col) followed by the first line of its source text; a parse
error carries name:  before its message. The decoration never changes the
error object that except matches.

(trace body…) evaluates its body and yields the last value. If an error
escapes, it yields the final data form(:trace (error :oops 1) frames=((name="/tmp/t.air" line=1 col=1 text="(def (bad ?x) (raise :oops x))")))

instead of throwing: the first element is the error object an except would
see, and frames lists the source frames known for it (() when none). The
result is final, so neither the error object nor the frames are re-reduced;
nested trace forms simply see the outer result as data. Use it to inspect a
failure without stopping a load or test.

A job is work that air runs later, in its own task, from a durable record.
Four special forms schedule one:

form

when it runs

body

(do-at time body…)

at a wall-clock time

a do block

(do-in interval body…)

after an interval, in seconds

a do block

(tx-at time body…)

at a wall-clock time

one transaction

(tx-in interval body…)

after an interval, in seconds

one transaction

and (task body… durable=true) registers a durable task instead of an
ephemeral one. Every scheduled call returns a promise; (await p) yields
the body’s value, and the promise is delivered exactly once.(val p (do-in 30 (check-widgets)))
(await p)                       ; => the value of (check-widgets)

Note

Nothing starts a job after a restart until air resumes it. See


Durability and resume.

The time argument of do-at/tx-at is a 

time value or a number of
UTC epoch seconds; a time in the past fires at once. The interval argument of
do-in/tx-in is a non-negative number of seconds. The body is every
positional form after the time together with the block’s let= and catch=
entries, so an event body is an ordinary do block:(do-in 5 let=(n=3) catch=true (print n) (throw :done))

do-in fires once. repeat=true turns it into a fixed-delay recurrence: the
next run is scheduled interval seconds after the previous one completes,
and missed occurrences coalesce rather than catch up. do-at and tx-at
reject repeat= — use do-in or tx-in to repeat.

tx-at/tx-in evaluate the body as one tx: an escaping error aborts every
write, and an error the body catches itself commits. Otherwise they behave
exactly like do-at/do-in.

The promise settles when a run finishes:

success delivers the body’s value (for do-in repeat=true, the first
run’s value; later runs do not deliver again);

an error delivers the air error object — (await p) returns (error …)
rather than raising, so a failed body is inspectable;

a cancellation delivers (error :event-cancelled name=…) or
(error :task-cancelled name=…);

a result the database cannot hold is delivered as
(error :un-storable …); the body’s other effects stand.

The status write and the delivery share one transaction, so a job cannot record
:done with an undelivered promise.

(val p (do-in 3600 name=:check-widgets (check-widgets)))
(events)                    ; => (check-widgets=(status=:pending …))
(event :check-widgets)      ; one summary, or (error :event-not-found …)
(cancel-event :check-widgets)
(cancel-event p)            ; the promise names the same job

form

meaning

(events [user])

a map name → summary of the user’s events

(event x [user])

one summary; x is a name (keyword, symbol, or string) or a promise

(cancel-event x [user])

cancel; returns the summary

(events-resume [user])

start every non-terminal event; (resumed=n)

The same four exist for durable tasks: tasks, task-info, cancel-task,
and tasks-resume.

A summary excludes the body and the captured context; it reports id, name,
kind, tx, owner, status, at, interval, repeat, attempts,
delivered, promise, result, error, and the timestamps.

A name must be free at creation; reusing a name whose record is still
:pending or :running raises an event-exists (or task-exists) error. A
terminal record’s name may be reused — the newer entry shadows it, and (events) lists only the
newest name. An unnamed call gets a generated name (e-… or t-…).

Cancelling settles the promise at once and stops a running body at its next
cancellation point: the reducer checks the attempt’s cancellation token every
64 reduction steps, and the whole-tree verbs (map, where, replace, sort,
…) check it every 1024 elements. It is not preemption in the stronger sense: a
body blocked in an uninterruptible call — a Julia extern, a database round trip,
a tensor computation, a blocking stream fetch or promise await — finishes
that call first, and
work the body spawned on another task with (task …) is not reached at all,
because cancellation does not cross a task boundary. A write the body committed
before the check stays committed, and the stopped attempt’s outcome is
discarded. Cancelling a terminal job is an idempotent no-op.

A val binding is task-local, so a job would normally see only definition
values. bindings= carries the creating task’s overrides into the new task:

value

effect

absent

no overrides (an event), the creator’s current overrides (a task)

true

snapshot the creator’s current overrides

false

no overrides

(x=1 y=sm)

exactly these values(val x 10)
(bind (x=99) (do-in 5 bindings=true (print x)))   ; prints 99
(do-in 5 bindings=(x=42) (print x))               ; prints 42
(do-in 5 (print x))                               ; prints 10

Bindings are captured as data, not as Var identity, so they survive a
serialization and a restart: the values are stored in the job record and
resolved by name when the run starts. An event therefore sees the values as of
creation, not as of firing. A name in an explicit mapping must be a val in
the creating context, and its value must be storable in the job’s database — a
mistake raises at creation, not hours later.

A stream is a durable value (it serializes as a link), so scheduling work that
posts to a stream is a first-class pattern:(val s (stream))
(do-in 60 bindings=(s=s) (post s "tick"))   ; the event posts a minute later

(task body… durable=true name=:nightly) registers the same kind of record
under $.config.tasks, starts it at once, and returns its promise. Plain
task remains ephemeral: its promise is durable, the running task is not.
bindings= defaults to true for both; name= requires durable=true, and
clean=true still clears .env and the bindings.

A durable task reruns from the start after a restart. (checkpoint form)
marks a step whose value a previous attempt already recorded, so the rerun
skips it:(task durable=true name=:nightly
      (checkpoint (fetch-source))
      (checkpoint (transform (checkpoint-value)))
      (store result))

Inside a durable run, checkpoint returns the recorded value when an earlier
attempt reached that point and otherwise evaluates its form, records the
result, and returns it. Outside a durable run — a plain task, an event, the
top level — it simply evaluates the form, so one body can serve every surface.
It refuses to run inside an open transaction, because its in-memory cursor
cannot roll back with a retried transaction.

Replay is at least once: a crash between an external side effect and the
checkpoint that records it repeats that step, and the sequence of checkpoint
call sites must be deterministic across attempts. The record is cleared when a
run completes, so a later resume starts clean.

A job’s record is a database value: a mapping holding its identity, kind,
owner, body, captured context, schedule, status, attempts, checkpoints, result,
error, and promise. It lives in the creating user’s home — $.config.events or
$.config.tasks — so a job belongs to the user who scheduled it, not to
whatever namespace happened to be current.

A job runs only while a process is alive. On startup, air calls the resume
machinery before the REPL and before serving:

a record left :running by a crash is flipped back to :pending and rerun
from the start (replaying its checkpoints);

a repeating event fires once and re-arms;

a due one-shot fires at once.

Embedders and tests get no implicit background work; call
(events-resume)/(tasks-resume) explicitly. It counts every non-terminal
record it made active, as (resumed=n).

Warning

Jobs are coordinated within one process. Two live processes over one database
are not: a cancel written by one is not seen by the other’s worker, and a
pending promise loaded in another live process is not woken by a delivery
there. Treat a registry as owned by one process at a time and poll (event …)
when crossing a process boundary.

Wall-clock due times can fire early or late if the system clock jumps. A
waiting job wakes four times a second to notice a cancel, so there is one
polling task per job.

A job is created and run with the identity of the user who scheduled it: the
body’s (current-user) is that user, and the record carries an owner-only ACL.
(events)/(tasks) filter to the records the caller can read, and another
user cannot inspect or cancel someone else’s job by name. air bypasses every
check; an admin sees its constituents’ jobs. A job cannot be created inside an
open transaction.

A body cannot resume mid-stack; a durable task reruns from the start and
relies on checkpoints.

Cancellation stops air evaluation at its next cancellation point (every 64
reduction steps, every 1024 elements of a whole-tree verb); it cannot
interrupt a long Julia call, and it does not cross a task boundary.

No cron syntax, retry policy, or backoff; a repeating job re-arms on a fixed
delay and a failed run simply records its error.

Reusing a terminal name accumulates a shadowed entry; there is no purge.

One polling task and one transaction per status change per job.

Worked solutions to the 25 problems in the 

problem set, written in air and
checked against the interpreter. Each entry gives the air code and a status:

✓ — works as written.

⚠ — works, with a caveat noted inline.

✗ — cannot be written with the current system; the blocking gap is named.

Everything here runs against an in-memory database (MemoryDatabase), so no
Postgres is needed; only the STM examples in Tier 4 need env.db.

Two syntax notes that the examples rely on: a :name is a keyword (inert
data), while a hold is a container headed by the symbol ' — (' a b c) —
and 'x is sugar for (' x) when x is a scalar, so (' a b) stays held as
data. Inside a hold, ~e (sugar for (preval e)) is substituted with the value
of e ((let (x=2) (' a ~x b)) → (' a 2 b); a let, however, substitutes its
names textually, so (let (x=2) (' a x b)) → (' a 2 b) too). (let (x=1 y=2) body…) binds in parallel and substitutes the values into the body before
evaluating it; a sequence of mappings, (let ((a=1) (b=2)) body…), lets each
group feed the next. (get c i) is the one accessor: an integer indexes a
sequence (1-based), a keyword a map, so a held form’s content starts at index 2
((get (' f a b) 2) is f). hold=true makes the root hold transparent, keeps
the extracted part held, and walks the path without reducing the intermediates;
(with form k1 … kn val hold=true) is the inverse, replacing a subpart with
val inserted without its own hold. The hold- family (hold-get,
hold-with, …) is the same treatment with the result held, and >> builds a
pipeline with _ as the placeholder ((x >> (_ + 1) (f _))).

records.content:
Unification is written in air itself: terms are ordinary forms held raw by the
rule parameters, variables are wildcards (?x), and a substitution is a map from
:x to its value.# ---- Mini-Prolog: unification ------------------------------------------------

(def (deref ?t ?s) hold=(t)
  (if (and (wildcard? t) (haskey s (keyword (name t))))
      (let (v=(get s (keyword (name t))))
        (deref v s))
      t))

(def (bind-var ?v ?t ?s)
  (join s ~(keyword (name v))=t))

(def (term-equal ?a ?b) hold=(a b)
  (if (seq? a)
      (if (seq? b)
          (if (== (count a) (count b))
              (loop (i 1)
                (if (i > (count a))
                    true
                    (let (ai=(get a i) bi=(get b i))
                      (if (term-equal ai bi)
                          (recur (i + 1))
                          false))))
              false)
          false)
      (if (seq? b) false (eq? (unhold a) (unhold b)))))

(def (unify-list ?xs ?ys ?i ?s) hold=(xs ys)
  (if (i > (count xs))
      s
      (let (xi=(get xs i) yi=(get ys i))
        (let (s2=(unify xi yi s))
  (if (eq? s2 :fail)
              :fail
              (unify-list xs ys (i + 1) s2))))))

(def (unify ?a ?b ?s) hold=(a b)
  (let (da=(deref a s) db=(deref b s))
    (if (and (wildcard? da) (wildcard? db) (term-equal da db))
        s
        (if (wildcard? da)
            (bind-var da db s)
            (if (wildcard? db)
                (bind-var db da s)
                (if (and (seq? da) (seq? db))
                    (if (== (count da) (count db))
                        (unify-list da db 1 s)
                        :fail)
                    (if (term-equal da db) s :fail)))))))

# ---- Mini-Prolog: resolution -------------------------------------------------

(def (rename-term ?t ?tag) hold=(t)
  (if (wildcard? t)
      (symbol (str "?" (name t) tag))
      (if (seq? t)
          (map (?e -> (rename-term e tag)) t)
          t)))

(def (push-goals ?q ?b)
  (loop (i (- (count b) 1) acc q)
    (if (i < 2)
        acc
        (recur (i - 1) (push acc (get b i))))))

(def (vars ?t ?acc) hold=(t)
  (if (wildcard? t)
      (if (member? t acc) acc (push acc t))
      (if (seq? t)
          (reduce ((?acc ?e) -> (vars e acc)) acc t)
          acc)))

(def (project ?vset ?s)
  (reduce ((?acc ?v) -> (join acc ~(keyword (name v))=(deref v s)))
          ()
          (drop-first 2 vset)))

(def (sol-count ?ss) (if (symbol? ss) 0 (- (count ss) 1)))
(def (sol-get ?ss ?i) (get ss (i + 1)))
(def (sol-add ?ss ?s) (if (symbol? ss) (sols s) (push ss s)))
(def (sol-merge ?a ?b)
  (loop (i 1 acc a)
    (if (i > (sol-count b))
        acc
        (recur (i + 1) (sol-add acc (sol-get b i))))))

(def (solve-clauses ?i ?acc ?g ?q ?db ?tag ?s ?vset)
  (loop (i i acc acc)
    (if (i > (count db))
        acc
        (let (c=(get db i))
          (let (tag2=(str tag "_" i))
            (let (h0=(get c :head))
              (let (b0=(get c :body))
                (let (h=(rename-term h0 tag2))
                  (let (b=(rename-term b0 tag2))
                    (let (s2=(unify g h s))
                      (recur (i + 1)
                             (if (eq? s2 :fail)
                                 acc
                                 (sol-merge acc (solve-q (push-goals q b) db tag2 s2 vset))))))))))))))

(def (solve-q ?q ?db ?tag ?s ?vset)
  (if (== (count q) 2)
      (sol-add sols (project vset s))
      (let (n=(count q))
        (let (g=(get q n))
  (let (q2=(wout q n))
  (solve-clauses 2 sols g q2 db tag s vset))))))

(def (solve ?goal ?db) hold=(goal)
  (solve-q (goals :done goal) db "" () (vars goal (vs :done))))

A database is a clauses form of head=/body= maps; each body is a goals
form headed by the goals marker and ending with a :done sentinel, which the
goal stack uses to detect the end of the search. The query is a raw term —
solve’s hold=goal parameter receives it exactly as written, so it is not
reduced:(let (db=(clauses
          (head=(parent :abe :bob) body=(goals :done))
          (head=(parent :bob :carl) body=(goals :done))
          (head=(ancestor ?x ?y) body=(goals (parent ?x ?y) :done))
          (head=(ancestor ?x ?y) body=(goals (parent ?x ?z) (ancestor ?z ?y) :done))))
  (solve (ancestor :abe ?who) db))
# => (sols (who=:bob) (who=:carl))

solve returns every solution — (ancestor ?a ?b) yields all three ancestor
pairs — and the bare symbol sols when there are none. Resolution is
depth-first with backtracking driven by iterating the clauses; each clause
invocation is freshened with a tag taken from its recursion path (symbol
builds names like ?x_3_2 at runtime), and term-equal compares terms
structurally without reducing them, so (1 + 2) is data rather than 3.

What the code exercises: hold= on def parameters passes a term into a
function unreduced; ~(keyword (name v))=… is a computed map key; and the
sentinels (:done, sols, (vs :done))
mark the end of the search. One sharp edge: a bound variable must
not share its name with the head of its own value. (let (db=db) db) is fine —
replacing db by itself is a fixed point and yields db — but a non-trivial
value such as (let (db=(db 1)) db) re-resolves its head db to the value again
until the recursion limit, hence the clauses marker above.

This document summarizes the architectural strategy for managing ephemeral, host-level execution resources (such as promises, tasks, and sockets) as extern types within Air, and how they interact with the persistence layer (AirDB.jl).

Extern Types: Low-level system resources and concurrency primitives are implemented as specialized Julia types managed directly by the host language’s garbage collector (GC).

First-Class In-Memory Representation: In-memory Air forms can seamlessly contain live Julia object references as leaf nodes, allowing operations like (await p) to execute with native performance.

Extensibility: Extern types are defined statically at startup via user-defined Julia methods implementing the Air extern protocol.

Because active sockets and in-flight tasks cannot be serialized as raw pointers to PostgreSQL, extern objects participate in a clean serialization protocol mapped to structured S-expressions in JSONB.

Serialized Form Shape:(extern :type payload)

Deserialization: When loaded from AirDB.jl, the runtime dispatches the form back through the registered startup extern methods to reconstruct the appropriate state or wrapper.

To avoid complex, race-prone asynchronous database row-mutations for in-flight tasks:

Ephemeral Resource Rule: Active, unresolved execution primitives are treated strictly as runtime execution state rather than permanent domain state.

The Tombstone Approach: When an active or pending extern object (such as an unfulfilled promise) hits the database serializer during a write/commit, it is immediately converted into an inert, serializable tombstone:(extern :promise :abandoned)

Behavior on Recovery: If application code encounters an expired or abandoned extern tombstone post-recovery, it fails cleanly with a structured runtime error (e.g., :extern-expired) rather than hanging indefinitely.

The concurrency primitives that can be persisted are not externs at all: they
are AirDB reference forms with their own serializations, and AirLang exposes one
constructor per kind.

air form

AirDB form

JSON

(actor value history=…)

ActorForm

"!<uuid>"

(promise)

PromiseForm

"~<uuid>" until delivered, then its value

(delay body…)

DelayForm(:air, cell)

{"delay": ":air", "form": "@<cell>"}

Actors. (send a fn) calls fn with the current value and persists the
result; inside a transaction the send is deferred to commit, and (sync)
flushes. The send captures the caller’s lexical names like a task (inner
binders shadow) and keeps the sender’s namespace layers and val bindings.
(reset! a value) replaces the value directly. Every update is
written to form_actor_current (plus form_actor_history when history is
on, fixed at creation).

Promises. (deliver p v) fills a promise once; (get p)/(await p)
read it (blocking outside a transaction, raising inside one unless it is
already delivered) and (ready? p) tests it. A promise stores a row and
always encodes as a link, whether it is pending or delivered, so a reader
waits on the same promise rather than on a copy of its value.

Delays. The registration registry (register_delay) is keyed by a type
name, and the loader sees only the serialized form. AirLang registers :air
once at startup; its serialization is a VolatileForm cell. The cell first
holds a tagged thunk — the substituted body plus the captured namespace path,
active using layers, val bindings, @ root, and .env — and is replaced
by the computed value on the first force. That is what makes the cache durable:
a fresh process that opens the database finds the value already computed and
never runs the body. The Env the force runs in is installed task-locally for
the dynamic extent of the call (the loader has no environment argument), and
the body runs as the user who forces it, like a stored def. A value the
database cannot hold, or a user without write access, is simply not cached;
the delay still yields the value. Printing and encoding never force a delay,
and a body that forces its own delay raises a catchable
(error :internal "a delay cannot force itself").

Most externs wrap a live resource and must die with the process. bytes is the
opposite: an opaque, immutable octet string that persists, compares by
content, and prints opaquely.(bytes "hello")            ; from a string's bytes
(bytes-of (104 105))       ; from a sequence of integers
(bytes-length b)           ; the octet count
(bytes-string b)           ; the raw octets as a string
(bytes-index b 1)          ; one octet as an integer (1-based)
(bytes-slice b 2 3)        ; a sub-range, as bytes
(bytes? x)

Because it is immutable and its equality is structural, two bytes values with
the same contents are the same air value: eq? and hash agree, so it works as
a memo key and in a keyed table. Its registration supplies serialize
(write(io, data)), deserialize (read(io)), equal, and hash to
register_extern, so a database stores and reloads the raw octets. It does
not round-trip through to-json/from-json: those write an unnamed extern
as an opaque marker, and reading it back yields a DeadExtern. Move a payload
through a database or an SFTP transfer instead. Printing is opaque —
#<bytes 1048576> — so a file-sized payload never floods a result or a log.

It is the value a transferred file becomes and the value a local file is read
back from: the SSH subsystem (

SSH access) turns a remote path into a
namespace path and a file into a bytes val.

A 

table is the second immutable, content-valued extern. It holds
persistent columns (FormSeq views over Air’s PVectors), an ordered name
list, a per-column _ColumnMeta (type and NA marker), a row count, and an
optional index dictionary. The registration supplies serialize, deserialize,
equal, and hash, so a committed table reloads with its schema and NA markers
intact, and eq?/hash agree on tables whose columns are in a different order
or whose cells are equivalent.

Like bytes, a table is stored faithfully in a database but does not survive
to-json/from-json text; for interchange use CSV/TSV or a database.

A 

tensor is the first mutable extern: an N-dimensional
Julia array over air’s numeric tower. Mutation is the reason for the
reservation protocol. An in-place write cannot be rolled back, so it may never
happen inside a transaction; instead AirDB’s extern protocol supplies two
operations, both surfaced in air:

reserve_read takes read locks, checks the extern versions, and runs the body
inline — safe inside a transaction, because a concurrent write forces a retry.
This is (reserve-read …) and {t : …}.

reserve takes write locks on a spawned task and returns an ExternPromise;
inside a transaction it is commit-gated. This is (reserve …) and
{t :! …}, and the promise is the air AirReservation (get/await/
ready?).

The extern registration is immutable-flagged false and supplies no codec,
equivalence, or constructor hooks: a tensor has no database identity, so it is
rejected as un-storable in a database namespace and reads back as a dead extern
through to-json. tensor->form is the portable spelling.

Status of §3. The tombstone scheme is not what the runtime does today: an
unnamed extern is written without an id and reads back as a DeadExtern that
prints #<extern :type (expired)> and raises (error :extern-expired :type)
when touched. A task returns a database PromiseForm, so its promise
survives a round trip (as a link until delivered); the running task itself is a
process item and cannot be serialized, so a promise whose task never delivered
is simply never delivered.

air reads and writes six text formats — JSON, YAML, TOML, CSV, TSV, and
.env — as plain air data. An object or table becomes a map form, an array
a sequence form, and a scalar a scalar; CSV and TSV decode to a


table and encode from one. Nothing else becomes an extern type,
and nothing in a file is ever executed. Decoding is therefore safe: a YAML file
cannot construct an object or call a function, however its tags are written.(decode "{\"a\": [1, 2], \"b\": null}" format=:json)   # => (a=(1 2) b=naught)
(encode (a=(1 2) b=naught) format=:json)               # => "{\"a\":[1,2],\"b\":null}"

form

meaning

(decode x format=:json)

parse text (a string or bytes) into a form

(encode v format=:json)

encode a form as text

(read-data path)

read a file, inferring the format from its name

(read-data path format=:yaml)

read a file in an explicit format

(write-data path v)

encode v and write it to a file

(write-data path v format=:toml)

write in an explicit format

format accepts a keyword, a symbol, or a string, and yml and dotenv are
aliases of yaml and env. The default for decode and encode is :json.
read-data and write-data infer the format from the extension (.json,
.yaml, .yml, .toml, .csv, .tsv, or the file name .env) and raise
when they cannot.(read-data "config.toml")               # => (server=(host="localhost" port=8080))
(write-data "out.yaml" (a=1 b=(1 2)))   # writes "a: 1\nb:\n  - 1\n  - 2\n"

Like write-file, write-data defers the write to the transaction commit, so a
transaction that aborts writes nothing.

The path helpers are gated by the filesystem permission on .air.sys, and
a fresh instance grants it only to air: read-data and write-data refuse
any other identity with (:permission-denied :filesystem :read-data) until
air runs (chmod! .air.sys filesystem=(:alice)). Startup code and libraries
(which run as air) use them freely; a shared configuration value reaches a
user through a namespace or a database, not through a host path. decode and
encode touch no file — they read a string or a bytes value — and need no
permission. See 

users, homes, and permissions.

The formats differ in what they can express; the mapping to forms is the same.

data

air

object / table / mapping

a map form, (a=1 b="x")

array / sequence

a sequence form, (1 2 3)

a scalar

the scalar, 1, 2.5, true, "x"

null

naught

an empty object or array

naught

Because an empty object and an empty array both become naught, the round trip
is lossy for empty containers: {"a": {}} and {"a": []} both encode as
(a=naught), which writes back as {"a": null}. A list holding empties keeps
its length — [{}, []] is (naught naught) — but each element is null.

A map key is normalized to its text, so {1: "x"} and {"1": "x"} name the
same air key. In a form the key is the air keyword spelling, which is the text
with a leading :; the printer drops that colon, so keys read naturally. Two
keys that normalize alike are a duplicate and raise rather than silently
overwriting.

A value is plain data if it is a scalar, a string, a keyword or symbol (which
encode as their text), a sequence of plain data, or a map of plain data. A
container that mixes sequence elements and map entries ((f a=1)) has no
representation in any format and raises. So does an extern, a mutable, a
reference form, a rational, or a complex number. Map keys are emitted in sorted
order in every format, so encoding is deterministic.

A 

table is the one extern with a plain-data shape: it encodes as
an array of its row maps, [{"a":1,"b":"x"},{"a":2,"b":"y"}]. Decoding that
returns the row maps, not a table — the schema is not carried by JSON or YAML —
so use CSV/TSV when a table needs to round-trip.(encode (name="x" count=1) format=:json)     # => "{\"count\":1,\"name\":\"x\"}"
(encode (1 a=2) format=:json)                # a map and a sequence in one form: error
(encode (/ 1 3) format=:json)                # a rational has no data representation: error

The reader is strict RFC 8259: objects, arrays, strings with the standard
escapes and \u surrogate pairs, true/false/null, and numbers with no
leading zero, trailing decimal point, or stray text. A duplicate key, an
unpaired surrogate, a truncated document, or trailing garbage is an error.

An integer that fits Int64 decodes as an Int64, a larger one as a BigInt,
and a number with a fraction or exponent as a Float64. Encoding rejects a
non-finite float (inf, -inf, nan), because JSON has no spelling for one.(decode "[1, 2.5, true, null, \"x\\n\"]")       # => (1 2.5 true naught "x\n")
(decode "9223372036854775808")                  # a BigInt
(encode naught format=:json)                    # => "null"

The YAML reader covers the practical subset a configuration file uses and is
safe by construction:

block mappings and sequences (a: 1, - 1), with sequences permitted at the
indentation of their parent key;

flow mappings and sequences ({a: 1}, [1, 2]), which may span lines;

plain, single-quoted, and double-quoted scalars, with '' doubling and the
Julia-style escapes (\n, \t, \x, \u, \U, \N, \_, \L, \P);

block scalars — literal | and folded >, with the strip (-), clip, and
keep (+) chomping modes and explicit indentation indicators;

comments, anchors and aliases (&name / *name), the << merge key, and
multi-document streams (--- / ...);

the core-schema resolution of plain scalars.

In the core schema a plain ~/null is naught, true/false are booleans,
decimal, 0x, and 0o integers are integers, and .inf/.nan are floats.
Everything else — including yes/no/on/off (which YAML 1.1 treats as
booleans) and bare dates — stays a string, as YAML 1.2 says.(decode "a: [1, 2]\nb:\n  c: |\n    x\n    y\n" format=:yaml)
# => (a=(1 2) b=(c="x\ny\n"))
(decode "yes: 2026-10-30\n" format=:yaml)     # => (yes="2026-10-30")

Tags are never constructed. The core tags (!!str, !!int, !!float,
!!bool, !!null, !!map, !!seq) are understood and apply their type; any
other tag — !!python/object, !custom, a %TAG directive — is an error.
That is the whole safety property: a YAML file from an untrusted source can only
produce data.

The reader bounds its work: nesting deeper than 256 levels, more than one
million nodes (including the size an alias expands to), a tab in indentation, or
an unknown alias is an error. Anchors are expanded when an alias is read, so an
“alias bomb” fails at the node limit instead of exhausting memory.

A stream with more than one document needs documents=true, which returns them
as a sequence; an empty or comment-only stream is naught. The encoder writes
block style with sorted keys, and a multi-document stream cannot be encoded
(encode each document and join them yourself).(decode "---\na: 1\n---\nb: 2\n" format=:yaml documents=true)   # => ((a=1) (b=2))
(decode "a: !!int \"5\"\n" format=:yaml)                       # => (a=5)
(decode "a: !!python/object x\n" format=:yaml)                 # error: unsupported tag

TOML maps onto forms directly: a table is a map form, an array a sequence form,
and an inline table a nested map. The document itself must be a table, so the
top level of a decoded TOML file is always a map form (an empty document is
naught). Tables encode after the scalar entries, as [section] headers; an
array is written inline, with a map element as an inline table.

TOML has no null, so a naught value cannot be encoded; only the empty
document is naught.(decode "port = 8080\n[db]\nhost = \"x\"\n" format=:toml)
# => (db=(host="x") port=8080)
(encode (port=8080 db=(host="x")) format=:toml)
# => "port = 8080\n\n[db]\nhost = \"x\"\n"
(encode (a=naught) format=:toml)             # error: TOML has no null

TOML integers are 64-bit, so a BigInt outside that range raises. A float is
written as nan, inf, -inf, or a decimal that always keeps a fractional
part.

TOML has native dates, times, and datetimes, which have no counterpart among
air’s values. They decode as marker forms that carry the literal text:(decode "d = 2026-10-30\nt = 12:30:00\nk = 2026-10-30T12:30:00\n" format=:toml)
# => (d=(toml-date "2026-10-30") k=(toml-datetime "2026-10-30T12:30:00")
#     t=(toml-time "12:30:00"))

The markers are ordinary air data — a two-element form headed toml-date,
toml-time, or toml-datetime. Encoding one writes its text unquoted when the
text is a valid literal of that kind and raises otherwise, so a marker never
silently becomes a string. Any other form of the same shape is an ordinary map.

An offset date-time keeps its offset exactly as written, including a
trailing Z:(decode "k = 2026-10-30T12:30:00-08:00\n" format=:toml)
# => (k=(toml-datetime "2026-10-30T12:30:00-08:00"))
(decode "k = 2026-10-30T12:30:00Z\n" format=:toml)
# => (k=(toml-datetime "2026-10-30T12:30:00Z"))

The standard library’s parser rejects ±hh:mm and drops Z, so the reader
protects each bare offset date-time before parsing and restores the marker
afterward; a date-time inside a string or a comment stays string data.

A decode produces a 

table; an encode accepts a table or a
non-empty sequence of row maps. The parser is a dependency-free RFC 4180 state
machine over UTF-8 text, and the column and row delimiters are options.

option

decode

encode

header

absent: infer; true: the first record names the columns; false: :col1…:colN; (names…): explicit names, no header consumed

true (default) writes the names; false omits them; (names…) writes explicit labels

column-delimiter

one-character string; default , (\t for tsv)

same

row-delimiter

string; default LF, accepting CRLF/LF/CR; when given, only that string ends a record and CR/LF are data

same; default \n

types

per-column type override

per-column output coercion

na

per-column missing marker

per-column missing marker

columns

rejected (use header=(…))

select and order the output columns

index

declare the table’s index column

rejected(decode "name,age\nBob,51\nSue,42" format=:csv)     # => #table(2×2: name, age)
(schema (decode "name,age\nBob,51\nSue,42" format=:csv))
# => (age=(na=NA type=:int) name=(na=NA type=:string))
(decode "1,2\n3,4" format=:csv)                     # => #table(2×2: col1, col2)
(encode (table a=(1 2) b=("x" "y")) format=:csv)    # => "a,b\n1,x\n2,y\n"
(encode ((a=1 b="x") (a=2 b="y")) format=:csv)      # the same text

Header inference. When header is absent, the first record is a header iff
no field in it is a plain number: a canonical integer spelling (no leading
zeros), or a finite Float64 (a fraction or exponent). Empty fields, NA, and
NaN do not count, so an all-string first row is a header and a row with any
number is data. This is a heuristic: a headerless all-string file loses its
first row, and a header row containing a numeric-looking field is treated as
data — pass header= whenever either is possible. header=false always names
the columns :col1…:colN, and header=("x" "y") names them explicitly
without consuming a record.

Parsing. A quote opens a quoted field only at its start; inside it a
doubled "" is a literal quote and every delimiter and newline is data. A quote
inside an unquoted field, text after a closing quote, or an unterminated field
raises, as does a record whose width differs from the header’s. CRLF, LF, and CR
all end a default-delimited record and a trailing terminator adds no row, so an
empty text is a 0-row table. Errors name the record number.

Types and NA. Fields are inferred with canonical rules: :int only for an
optional - and digits with no leading zero (so 007 stays a string), :float
only for a finite parse that is not an integer (so 1e3 is a float), :bool
only for true/false, and otherwise :string. types= overrides the
inference; declaring :string, :symbol, or :keyword keeps the field’s text,
while :int, :float, :number, and :bool parse it. An empty field is the
column’s NA, and the text NA or NaN is missing unless the column declares a
different marker with na=. A missing cell writes back as an empty field.(schema (decode "a,b\n1,2.5" format=:csv))
# => (a=(na=NA type=:int) b=(na=NaN type=:float))
(get (decode "a\n007\n1e3\ntrue\nNA" format=:csv) :a)
# => ("007" 1000.0 true NA)
(decode "n,a\nBob,1\nSue,2" format=:csv index=:n)   # an indexed table
(encode (table a=(1 NA) b=(NaN 2.0)) format=:csv)   # => "a,b\n1,\n,2.0\n"
(encode (table a=(1 2)) format=:csv columns=(:a) header=false)   # => "1\n2\n"

TSV is not the IANA backslash convention. It is RFC 4180 quoting with a tab
column delimiter: a tab, a newline, or a " inside a field is quoted by doubling
the quotes, exactly as for CSV.

What is lost. CSV carries no types of its own: a symbol or keyword decodes as
a string unless types= says otherwise, a "007" field stays a string, and a
naught cell cannot be spelled (declare an na= and use it, or encode a
different format). Encoding a naught cell, a container cell, or a non-finite
float that is not the column’s NA raises.

A .env file is a flat mapping of variable names to text. Decoding accepts
comments, blank lines, an export  prefix, and empty, single-quoted,
double-quoted, and bare values; an unquoted # after whitespace starts a
comment, and \n, \t, \\, \", and \' are recognized in double quotes.
A name must be a letter or _ followed by letters, digits, _, ., or -.
Duplicate names and a line that is not name=value raise.

Every value is a string — .env has no numbers, booleans, or nulls — so
A=1 decodes as (A="1"). Encoding requires a map at the top level whose
values are scalars; a naught value writes an empty value, and a value needing
quotes is double-quoted.(decode "export A=1\nB=\"x y\"\n" format=:env)     # => (A="1" B="x y")
(encode (B="x y" A="1") format=:env)               # => "A=1\nB=\"x y\"\n"
(encode (a=(1 2)) format=:env)                     # error: .env values are strings

Note that .env keys are conventionally uppercase, but air does not enforce or
change case: (A="1") writes A=1 and (a="1") writes a=1.

Databases describes AirDB’s to-json and from-json, which
also produce text. They are a serialization codec: a volatile becomes a
"@uuid" link, a non-finite float is the marked string "#inf", and a cycle is
legal. encode/decode are a data codec: every value is written out
literally, links are not followed, and a non-finite float or a cyclic value is
an error. Use to-json to move air values between databases and encode to
exchange plain data with another program.

JSON nesting is bounded at 512 levels; YAML at 256, with a one-million-node
total.

JSON, YAML, TOML, and .env round-trip plain, non-empty data exactly under
eq?; decode(encode(x)) is not x for an empty container, which becomes
naught, or for a TOML date marker written to another format, which becomes a
map or a string. A table round-trips through CSV/TSV with its schema, but a
symbol, keyword, or "007" field returns as a string unless types= names
the column’s type.

There is no spreadsheet reader (.xlsx and friends) yet; CSV and TSV are
covered above.

Julia 1.11 or later. AirLang’s Project.toml uses the [sources] local
path entries that Julia 1.11 introduced.

Air.jl 0.3 and
AirDB.jl 0.1, checked out beside
this repository. AirLang depends on both as local path packages.

PostgreSQL only if you want database-backed persistence. The default
in-memory database needs no server.

Clone the three repositories as siblings. AirLang’s Project.toml resolves
../Air.jl and ../AirDB.jl, so the directory names matter:mkdir -p ~/Code && cd ~/Code

Pkg.instantiate() resolves the path dependencies and downloads the registered

bin/air is the command line. With no arguments it starts a read-eval-print
loop; -e evaluates one chunk of code; any other argument is a file to load:./bin/air                              # the REPL
./bin/air -e '(+ 1 2)'                 # => 3
./bin/air -e 'using AirLang; (println "hi")'
./bin/air program.air                  # load a file
./bin/air --serve program.air          # load, then stay up (ssh-server, …)

--serve keeps the process alive after the files and -e chunks are
evaluated, so an ssh-server (or another process resource) keeps serving until
SIGINT or SIGTERM. This is how the Docker container stays up.

The -e chunks and files in one invocation share an environment, so definitions
made by an earlier -e are visible to a later one. The REPL reads a form across
lines while the reader reports an unterminated form, string, or block comment
(with a ...>  continuation prompt) and sets AIR_HISTORY to a file that each
complete input is appended to, for use with external line editors such as
rlwrap.

From Julia, the same entry points are available as functions:using AirLang, AirDB

env = Env(db = MemoryDatabase())          # a private in-memory database
air_eval(env, read_air("(+ 1 2)"))        # => 3

At the REPL, (help) prints an introduction to the language, (doc NAME)

The repository ships a Dockerfile and a docker-compose.yml. The image is a
slim Julia runtime with AirLang and its dependencies precompiled; it contains no
build toolchain, and the host’s ./lib is mounted at /air/lib and used as the
library path.

The sibling checkouts are passed as named build contexts (BuildKit, the default
in current Docker):docker build -t airlang \
    --build-context air=../Air.jl \
    --build-context airdb=../AirDB.jl .

Or use the compose file, which names the same contexts, starts a PostgreSQL
sidecar, and brings up air as an SSH server:docker compose up -d --build         # air (SSH on :2222) plus PostgreSQL
docker compose up -d --wait          # ...and block until air is listening
docker compose logs -f air           # follow the air log
docker compose down                  # stop both; the database volume survives

docker compose up -d publishes port 2222 at once but air takes a few seconds
to load the interpreter and evaluate startup.air before it listens. A
connection in that window is accepted by Docker’s proxy and reset during key
exchange, so ssh reports an immediate close; --wait blocks on the compose
healthcheck until the port answers, and ssh -v shows the same window as
kex_exchange_identification: read: Connection reset by peer.

docker compose up -d runs air --serve startup.air in the container; add
--build on the first run and after changing the image’s source. The
repository’s startup.air opens the PostgreSQL sidecar as the namespace .db,
creates an example user with a placeholder SSH key, and starts
(ssh-server :sshd port=2222 bind="::"); compose publishes port 2222 and mounts
./lib at /air/lib, the first AIR_LIBPATH entry. Edit startup.air to set
your own user name and public key (replace the base64 blob with the contents of
~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub), then docker compose restart air. Log in with:ssh -p 2222 <your-user>@localhost

:: is dual-stack: ssh localhost tries ::1 before 127.0.0.1, and a server
bound only to 0.0.0.0 (IPv4) leaves Docker’s proxy with nowhere to send the
IPv6 attempt, which the client reports as an immediate close during key
exchange. Every SSH refusal is silent on the wire by design; to see why one
failed, run JULIA_DEBUG=AirLang docker compose up -d and follow
docker compose logs -f air.

--serve is the one CLI flag the container needs: it runs the files and -e
chunks, then keeps the process alive so its ssh-server (and any other process
resource) keeps serving until SIGINT/SIGTERM ends it.

One-off commands use the same image and mounts:docker compose run --rm air -e '(+ 1 2)'   # => 3

bin/air-docker is a thin wrapper that runs the image with the same command
line as bin/air and mounts ./lib; it is the easy way to get an interactive
REPL:./bin/air-docker                     # REPL
./bin/air-docker -e '(+ 1 2)'        # => 3
./bin/air-docker program.air

Inside the container the library path is /air/lib (the mount) and Julia’s
depot is /opt/julia.

The test suite needs only the default in-memory database; the PostgreSQL tests
run when AIRLANG_TEST_PG_URL names a server:julia --project=. test/runtests.jl

# ... with PostgreSQL:
AIRLANG_TEST_PG_URL="postgresql://air:air@localhost/air" \
    julia --project=. test/runtests.jl

julia --project=. -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.test()' is the same suite under Pkg’s
isolation. The docker-compose.yml sidecar provides a PostgreSQL server with
user, password, and database air:docker compose up -d postgres

Air is a Clojure- and Mathematica-inspired scripting language that runs on
Julia. It is implemented by AirLang.jl, which builds on two libraries:

Air.jl — Clojure-like immutable
data structures and a software transactional memory (STM); and

AirDB.jl — a persistence layer
that stores Air forms in PostgreSQL jsonb tables in transaction order.

Air’s two rule systems make it a natural interface to a reasoning and rules
system: one evaluates code by term rewriting (def, replace, lambdas), and
the other derives and maintains facts in a logic set (assert, rule,
query). Everything — code, data, rules, and errors — is the same kind of
immutable, inspectable form.

The short version

Air is a Lisp whose values are JSON-like forms, whose functions are rewrite
rules, whose namespaces are multi-user logic sets persisted in PostgreSQL, and
whose errors are matched structurally rather than by class.

(+ 1 2)                             # => 3
(let (x=2 y=3) (* x y))             # => 6
(thread (f (1 2 3)))                # => ((f 1) (f 2) (f 3))
(replace ((a 1) (a 2)) ((a ?x) -> x) depth=1)   # => (1 2)

Definitions are patterns, and the body is a replacement:(def (fact ?n)
  (if (< n 2) 1 (* n (fact (- n 1)))))

(fact 5)                            # => 120

Facts and rules live in a namespace, which is implicitly a logic set:(namespace .app)
(assert .app (depends :app :lib1))
(assert .app (rule (depends ?x ?y) :> (needs ?x ?y)))

(facts .app)                        # => (' (depends :app :lib1) (needs :app :lib1))
(query .app (needs ?x ?y))          # => ((x=:app y=:lib1))

before it, and the table of contents is a reasonable reading order end to end.

Air.jl 0.3 and

A PostgreSQL server is needed only for database-backed work; the default
in-memory database needs nothing. See

Note

The reference documentation describes the language as implemented by AirLang.jl.
Some parts of the wider design — notably the incremental RETE network and
sequence patterns — are still deferred; they are listed under


Implementation status.

(load-air path…) evaluates every form in every named file, in order. It reads
and parses every file before evaluating any form, then evaluates inside
one transaction, so a parse error or a runtime error leaves nothing behind. It
returns the last value. A relative path resolves against the directory of the
file that contains the load-air call (the process working directory at top
level), not against the caller’s current directory:(load-air "util.air")   ; next to the loading file (or the cwd at top level)

The air command line uses the same loader: air file.air and air -e '…'.
The system namespace exposes the same functions as .air.sys.load-air,
.air.sys.read-file, and so on.

A library is a directory whose name is a valid name segment and that
contains an init.air. AIR_LIBPATH is a :-separated list of search
directories (; on Windows), read when a library is first needed; the default
is <repo>/lib and ~/.air/lib, and the first directory with a matching
<name>/init.air wins. A library loads lazily — when .lib.<name> is first
addressed, or when a bare using/import spec names it:(using math (twice 4))       ; loads <libpath>/math/init.air if needed
(.lib.math.twice 4)          ; same

init.air runs as air, with .lib.<name> as the current namespace and the
library directory as the loading directory, in one transaction under a
per-library lock. A failed load registers nothing ((.lib.bad …) raises the
error the file raised; .lib has no bad entry afterwards). A recursive
reference to a library already loading is declined rather than deadlocking.

Forms are immutable, but a form may contain a mutable: a shared reference
synchronized across threads, like Clojure’s ref and implemented by AirDB.
A mutable is a value like any other — it can be stored in a form, in a
namespace, or in a database — and every write to one happens in a transaction.
This chapter covers creating and editing a mutable, its filter and finalizer
hooks, watches, and the tx and sandbox block forms.

(mut value filter=… finalize=…) creates a mutable holding value.
(value m), (get m), and (get m 0) all read it; a mutable also vanishes
on a get path, so (get (a=<mutable>) :a :b) reads through it as if the
mutable were not there.(let (m=(mut 3)) (+ (get m) 1))     # => 4

mut? tests one. A mutable prints as #<volatile …>, and two reads of the
same mutable are the same object (same?); the value inside participates in
eq? only through the mutable’s identity (see 

Equality).

Every operation that edits a mutable in a transaction ends in !;
mut does not, because it creates rather than edits a volatile.(set! m 4)                     # replace the value
(set! form 2 :a 4)             # edit the deepest mutable on the path
(swap! m inc)                  # replace with (inc old), returning the new value
(swap! m + 10)                 # (fn value args…) in one transaction
(alter! m inc)                 # an alias of swap!

set! with more than two arguments walks a path and edits the deepest mutable
on it. swap!/alter! applies its function to the current value in a single
transaction and returns the new value, so a lost update is impossible. set!,
swap!, alter!, chmod!, and chown! are the volatile edits; reset! is
reserved for actors (see 

Actors).

(mut value filter=… finalize=…) attaches Air’s filter and finalizer. Both are
kept as written and stored in the mutable’s metadata, so they survive a reload.
A replacement rule (?x -> …) is applied as a function; any other form is
evaluated with _ bound to the value, so filter=(if (_ < 0) 0 _) clamps at
zero.

A filter runs on every write (including the value passed to mut) and its
result is stored. A finalizer runs after the body of the writing transaction
and before it commits, and its result replaces the value. Because the finalizer
runs in the transaction’s finalizing state, volatiles cannot be written from it.
(set-filter! m fn) and (set-finalize! m fn) replace them later (naught
removes one); (set! …) and these two are the ways to change a mutable.

(watch m key fn) registers fn to run as (fn key m old new) at the end of
the body of the outermost transaction that writes m, before it commits:(watch m :log (part println "changed:"))
(set! m 10)                    # => the watch runs once, before the commit
(unwatch m :log)               # remove one watch
(watches m)                    # the held watch tables

The watch runs as the user who registered it, in the namespace where it was
registered, and once per mutable per transaction (with the transaction’s
final value). Its writes are part of the same transaction, so a retry reruns
it; a raise from it aborts the transaction, while a throw is deferred like
any throw caught outside (see 

Errors and blocks). Watches are
stored in the mutable’s metadata and survive a reload; a watch function must be
self-contained (a replacement rule, not a code fragment using _). Installing a
watch needs watch and read on the mutable; watch is owner-only by default.

(tx body…) evaluates its body inside one STM transaction and yields its last
value. It accepts the full do block grammar — :let/let=, catch=/throw,
except, handle/notify, and finally — all prepared and run inside the
transaction.

Air’s transactions join rather than nest: tx joins an open transaction, so
the outermost tx is the commit/rollback boundary (namespace, load-air, a
logic-set edit, and set! are transactional too). An error that escapes it
aborts every write made since it began and propagates, even if an outer block
catches it; an error caught by the tx’s own except commits. A throw caught by
the tx’s own catch= commits. A throw that escapes the tx to an outer catch=
is deferred until after the commit: watches run as usual, the transaction
commits, and the signal is rethrown (a retried attempt discards it). Watches run
at the end of that outermost transaction body, so their writes commit or roll
back with it.

(sandbox body…) evaluates the same block grammar in a transaction that is
never committed: it yields the body’s value and discards every write, so a
def, val, mut, fact, rule, or namespace created inside it is gone
afterwards. It is the way to try something out — a rule you are not sure about,
a namespace edit you want to test — without touching the namespace. Because Air’s
transactions join rather than nest, the body runs in a transaction of its own on
a private task (the caller waits for it), which means it cannot abort a
transaction around it and it reads committed state rather than an enclosing
transaction’s staged writes. A throw still reaches an enclosing catch= and a
notify an enclosing handle; side effects outside the database (a file write,
open-airdb) are not undone.

(sync) waits for committed writes to reach the database, and (status) reports
the pending write count; see 

Sync and status.

A mutable belongs to the database of the namespace it is created in: mut
in .main makes a process-store mutable, while mut in a namespace under an
opened root makes one in that root’s database. A value assigned in a database
namespace must be storable; embedding a mutable from another database raises
(error :un-storable target). This is the same rule for every reference form
(see 

Databases).

Two related values look like mutables on the access path but are not written
with set!: a delay is a database-backed value computed once, and an
actor is a sequential worker written with send/reset!. Both are
described in 

Tasks, delays, actors, and promises.

Errors and blocks — the clause grammar tx and sandbox accept.

Databases — persistence, named forms, and sync.

Namespaces — the namespace a mutable is stored in.

A namespace is an ordered collection of def and val definitions addressed by
a dotted path. . alone is the global namespace root; .air is the core
namespace, holding every builtin, operator, standard-library name, and constant
(pi, e, tau, inf, nan). A leading-dot atom is a path:
.util.algebra.square reads as (get . :util :algebra :square), so the whole
namespace tree is ordinary . access over nested namespace values. A bare name
in a namespace form is a root-level name, so (namespace util …) is
(namespace .util …).

The root holds the process’s system namespaces:

path

contents

.air

the generated core namespace: builtins, operators, constants (owned by air, world r-x)

.air.sys

the system functions: load-air, read-file, write-file, read-data, write-data, open-airdb, close-airdb

.sys

system state; readable only by air

.sys.user.<name>

a system user’s record and home

.lib

the library cache (owned by air, world r-x)

.main

air’s startup namespace

.env

a val holding the task’s environment mapping

Every entry in a namespace is itself a volatile with its own metadata — owner,
ACL, provenance, and an optional anchor — so two users may own different
definitions in one namespace, and an import is an explicit, inspectable entry
rather than a transient lookup. Metadata is visible to anyone who can reach an
entry; the body is gated by its read permission (see 

Users, homes, and
permissions).(namespace .util
  (def (twice ?x) (* x 2))
  (val answer 42))
(.util.twice 4)      # => 8
(.util.answer)       # => 42

def and val inside a namespace block append to that namespace, and a
subnamespace is created automatically: (namespace .util.algebra (…)) registers
algebra inside .util (creating any missing ancestors). A namespace block is
a transaction — if a body form fails, everything the block defined rolls back. A
subnamespace may never shadow a definition of the same name, in either order, and
neither may a definition shadow a subnamespace.

Definitions added later are matched first, so a reload or override wins:(namespace .util (def (twice ?x) (* x 2)))
(namespace .util (def (twice ?x) (+ x x)))
(.util.twice 4)      # => 8, from the later definition

A zero-argument call applies a definition too: (.util.f) calls f, matching
either (def (f) …) or a scalar (def f …).

Roots, homes, and the current namespace

records.content:
Three addresses are resolved by the running task rather than by fixed paths:

$ — the current user’s home namespace: .sys.user.<u>.home for a system
user, @.user.<u>.home for a database user. It is a capability held directly
by the task, so a user works in their home without being able to read .sys
(or the user records enclosing it).

@ — the root namespace of the database the task is attached to. An
unattached user sees @ as . (the air root).

The current namespace — task-local: $ for a created user, .main for
air at boot. A top-level def/val is written there, so it is durable: an
entry in a namespace rather than a process-global rule. (namespace path body…) replaces the current namespace for body and does not layer the
caller’s definitions, which is what makes (namespace .air …) pristine;
using=(ns…) activates namespaces for the body without nesting it.

$ and @ are ordinary symbols: a lexically bound name shadows them and let
may rebind them ((let ($=8) $) → 8), so bind them as data, not as code.

A .-atom address is not the only spelling a namespace-taking form accepts.
(get $ :config) and a leading-. path name the same namespace, and every form
that resolves an address — namespace, using, use, import, unuse,
clear, open-airdb, and the logic-set targets — accepts either, so
(namespace $.config.ssh (val authorized-keys ("…"))) writes
.sys.user.<u>.home.config.ssh. The resolver checks a bound name first: when
the body has bound $ (or @) lexically, the form is evaluated normally and
the binding wins, exactly as it does for a bare $.

The task’s identity, current namespace, database root, and .env mapping
travel with spawned tasks, so a task sees the same roots (see


Tasks).

ns-entries lists a namespace’s entries as data, filtered by permission:(ns-entries .util)
# => ((entry name=:twice kind=:def owner=:air)
#     (entry name=:answer kind=:val owner=:air)
#     (entry name=:algebra kind=:sub owner=:air))
(ns-entries .util src=true)   ; each entry also carries src="…" when it has one
(ns-entry .util :twice)       ; one entry, or naught when it is absent

The optional target is a namespace path (the current namespace by default) and
src=true adds the definition’s stored source text. name is a keyword,
not a bare symbol, so listing an entry named after a definition returns the name
rather than reducing to that definition’s value. kind is :def, :val,
:sub (a subnamespace), :proxy (a lazily resolved import), or :alias;
doc= is present when the definition has a docstring, and owner= names the
entry’s owner.

Entries the caller may not read are absent, exactly as in using and doc
listings — never blanked or greyed, so an unreadable entry and a hided one look
identical to a name that does not exist. A subnamespace is listed only when its
own namespace is readable.

Three more listings name the definitions rather than describe them. ns-vals
returns the readable val names as keywords, newest definition last, with a
name redefined in the namespace appearing once at its last position. ns-defs
returns the readable def rules, each as its definition form held and with
def replaced by ':(namespace .util (val answer 42) (def (twice ?x) (* x 2)))
(ns-vals .util)   # => (:answer)
(ns-defs .util)   # => ((' def (twice ?x) (* x 2)))

Both default to the current namespace and accept the same target argument as
ns-entries. Any stored source position (src=) is stripped from a ns-defs
element; a docstring survives as a doc= entry. The facts and rules of a
namespace’s implicit logic set are listed by ns-facts and ns-rules, which
return the same held lists as (facts target) and (rules target); see


The two rule systems.

The namespace browser in 

User interfaces is a view over ns-entries.

(using spec… body…) activates one namespace, or a list of them, for body:
the namespace’s rules are searched (below body’s own definitions and above the
global store) and its vals become resolvable names. using copies nothing; it
is context for the body. A spec is a namespace address with optional only=,
except=, and as= options, written either as keyword pairs in the spec’s
sequence or in its map:(using .util (twice 4))
(using (.util :only (twice answer)) (twice 4))
(using (.util :except (answer)) (twice 4))
(using ((.util :only (twice)) (.util.algebra :as alg)) (get alg :square))

Later specs have priority over earlier ones. as= binds the namespace value
itself to a name (it does not add a dot path).

Inside a namespace block, (use spec…) and (import spec…) materialize
the selected names as entries of the current namespace. use keeps them private
(they compile into the namespace’s rules but are absent from its map); import
also exports them in the map. What is stored depends on what the importer may do
with the source entry:

source entry

stored entry

readable def

a copy, owned by the target namespace’s owner, carrying the source’s ACL

readable val

an entry that shares the source’s Var, so a rebinding of the source is visible

execute-only, a proxy, or anchor=true

a proxy storing (source path, name); it applies the source lazily with the source entry’s owner and ACL

subnamespace

a link entry, resolved through the source namespace

Every imported entry records source=<namespace> in its metadata. Re-importing
a name replaces the previous entry from that source, so an import is how a
namespace is refreshed. A proxy keeps an execute-only body hidden; a missing
source raises (error :proxy-unresolved path) at call time. (chmod! entry anchor=true) marks an entry so that it is always imported as a proxy, even when
it is readable.(namespace .algebra
  (use .util)                        ; may call (twice 2) inside this namespace
  (import (.util :only (answer)))    ; `answer` becomes part of `.algebra`
  (def (quad ?x) (* (twice (twice x)) 2)))
(algebra.quad 3)                     # => 24
(get . :algebra :answer)             # => 42

Removal:

(clear sym) removes the current block’s entries that define or export sym,
including imported copies; (clear :all) removes every definition and import
(local subnamespaces stay).

(unuse ns) removes the block’s entries imported from ns; (unuse ns name…) removes just those names (provenance is the entry’s source=).

(del sym) is an alias of clear. Outside a namespace block, clear targets
the process-global rule store and never removes a builtin, operator, or core
constant.

(val pattern form…) is like def, but form is evaluated once at definition
time and the pattern is installed as a value rather than a function — it cannot
be called. Each val is backed by an Air Var, so its value is thread-local:
a bind shadows it in the current task only and restores the previous value when
its body finishes. bind names values by the name its namespace context matches,
so it rebinds exactly the val that a bare reference would see:(val x 10)
(bind (x=99) x)                             # => 99
x                                           # => 10
(using .util (bind (answer=1) (twice 1)))   # => 3

The binding form is evaluated before it is used, so its values are ordinary
expressions ((bind (x=(x + 1)) x) → 11). Binding a name that is not a val in
the current context is an error. bind is dynamic, not lexical: it affects calls
into rules and namespace functions made within its body.

(bindings) evaluates to a mapping of the current task’s overrides — the vals
whose value differs from its definition value — and that mapping can be
reinstalled with bind:(bind (x=1 y=2) (bindings))     # => (x=1 y=2)
(bind (x=5) (bind (bindings) x))   # => 5
